docs.body:
# Scoreboard Leadership

*Part Two of a series on transformational and servant leadership*

## Eight is Great

John Stumpf grew up on a dairy farm in Minnesota, one of eleven children, and went to work in banking straight out of college. He joined Norwest Corporation in 1982 and spent the next three decades climbing through it, becoming president in 2005 and chief executive in 2007, the same year Norwest's successor, Wells Fargo, was about to be tested by the worst financial crisis in eighty years. Stumpf steered the bank through the acquisition of Wachovia during that crisis without the bailout drama that swallowed several of his competitors, and Wells Fargo came out the other side looking like the safest big bank in the country. In 2013, both Fortune and American Banker named Wells Fargo the least tarnished bank of its size, and American Banker crowned Stumpf its Banker of the Year.

The engine underneath that reputation had a name. Eight is Great, Stumpf's own shorthand for a target that wasn't actually a fixed list of eight named products. In a 2010 letter to shareholders, Stumpf wrote that the goal was eight products per customer because eight "rhymed with great." In practice, the number got filled however a branch could fill it, some combination of a checking account, a savings account, a car loan, a mortgage, a personal loan, a credit card, or another banking product, whatever mix got a household to eight. He called the whole approach cross-selling on earnings call after earnings call, and framed it publicly as deepening the customer relationship. For years it worked exactly as advertised. Analysts pointed to Wells Fargo's cross-sell numbers as a reason to buy the stock, and the value of Stumpf's own shares grew by more than two hundred million dollars while he made that case to investors.

## The number becomes the mission

Underneath the mantra was a mechanism, and the mechanism had teeth. Branch employees were monitored daily and sometimes hourly, their numbers reported up the chain to managers who pushed back down the same day. The pressure on employees is documented in the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's own Notice of Charges against former Wells Fargo executives. It found the bank's business model imposed "intentionally unreasonable sales goals and unreasonable pressure on its employees to meet those goals," enforced through daily or hourly monitoring, subjecting employees to what the OCC itself called "hazing-like abuse," and threatening to terminate, and actually terminating, employees who fell short. The same filing found the resulting turnover ran close to 35 percent annually, well above peer banks, a rate the OCC called evidence the sales pressure itself was excessive.

A separate lawsuit filed the same year, reported by Reuters, named former employees Alexander Polonsky and Brian Zaghi, who said managers pressed workers to meet quotas of ten accounts a day, demanded progress reports several times daily, and reprimanded anyone who fell short.

Employees who could not hit eight through honest sales started manufacturing it instead, and the manufacturing was not evenly distributed. Employees used customers' personal identification numbers without their knowledge to open products in their name, and reporting on the scandal found the victims were disproportionately elderly customers and Spanish speakers, the customers least likely to catch an extra account buried in a statement. By the time the pattern surfaced publicly, Wells Fargo employees had opened millions of accounts customers never asked for and never knew existed.

Wells Fargo told its own employees there was a proper channel for exactly this kind of concern, an internal ethics hotline called EthicsLine. Some employees noticed the fraud long before anyone outside the company did, and used that channel to try to stop it. Yesenia Guitron worked at a Wells Fargo branch in St. Helena, California, starting in 2008. She watched customers end up holding products they had never asked for, telling CBS News she saw "people ending up with 10-to-15 debit cards that they didn't request" tied to a single account. She raised it with her branch manager first. Nothing changed. She escalated to human resources and then to the company's own ethics department. She was fired. She later described the fight that followed as feeling like "this little me against a big powerful Wells Fargo bank."

Claudia Ponce de Leon had been promoted ten times over a decade at Wells Fargo, rising to branch manager on the strength of her performance. In 2011, she called the company's ethics hotline with concerns about the sales practices she was watching happen under her own roof. She was fired three weeks later. It took the Department of Labor until 2017 to order her reinstated with back pay, six years after she made the one call the company claimed to want employees to make.

Both women used the exact channel Wells Fargo told its own people to use, and both were removed for it, years before Congress ever asked Stumpf a single question. Wells Fargo fired roughly 5,300 employees over the fraud itself, almost all of them tellers and branch staff earning an hourly wage, not the executives who had set the target they were trying to survive. Two of those employees later sued, arguing they were fired for refusing to do the very thing the company's own incentive system was built to produce.

Congress asked Stumpf to account for it on the record. He resigned in October 2016. Regulators later found that Stumpf had ignored years of warning signs, including complaints that had already reached his own office, and never seriously examined the sales goals he had spent a decade defending to investors. The finding named the actual root cause: the business model itself, the unreasonable goals and the pressure built into hitting them. In 2020, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency banned Stumpf from the banking industry for life and fined him 17.5 million dollars, the largest individual penalty the agency had ever issued against a bank executive.

Stumpf did not fail because he lacked a method. He failed because the method he built had no room in it for anything but the number, and eventually the number ran straight through the people it was supposed to serve.

## What Scoreboard Leadership is

That is Scoreboard Leadership. Transactional leadership with the morality engineered out, the same removal Bernard Bass made to James MacGregor Burns's definition in 1985, covered in the last post. The number becomes the mission. Metrics stop being instruments for understanding the work and become weapons for extracting more of it. People stop being the point and become inputs, valued at exactly the rate they produce and discarded at the rate they stop. I coined the term and own the domain, ScoreboardLeadership.com, because this failure mode deserved a name of its own. When leadership becomes a game to win instead of a mission to serve, everyone eventually loses.

It is not limited to companies. It shows up anywhere a relationship gets reduced to output, though the clearest, most measurable evidence of it right now sits inside organizations, which is where this post will spend most of its time before circling back to what the same trade looks like closer to home.

## The end state

Amazon runs an internal system called ADAPT, short for Associate Development and Performance Tracker, that tracks each warehouse worker's productivity against a rate the company does not disclose to the worker. The system generates warnings automatically, without a supervisor reviewing the case first, and can recommend termination through that same pipeline. Amazon disputes how far the pipeline runs on its own. A company spokesperson has said "it is absolutely not true that employees are terminated through an automatic system," and maintains a manager always has final say before anyone loses a job.

## What the workers say

The people living inside the system describe something closer to the harder version of the story. Warehouse workers have testified that managers stay vague about what actually gets a person fired, which creates an ongoing sense of paranoia on the floor, and that breaks and injuries get sacrificed because falling behind the rate carries a more immediate, visible consequence than an aching back does. In one of the most detailed accounts on record, investigative journalist James Bloodworth spent six months working undercover in a Staffordshire, England fulfillment center and found that roughly 1,200 workers faced a ten-minute, nearly quarter-mile round trip just to reach the two nearest toilets. Workers described skipping the trip rather than risk being flagged for time away from the line.

Not every challenge to the system succeeded. Nicholas Stover, a former Amazon employee with Crohn's disease, was fired over what his supervisor called time theft, unscheduled bathroom breaks he needed because of his condition, and sued Amazon under the Americans with Disabilities Act. A federal court granted summary judgment for Amazon, and the Sixth Circuit affirmed that ruling in 2022, finding no evidence his termination was because of his disability and that he had not properly requested an accommodation even after Amazon asked for documentation. The case did not establish that Amazon's system was unlawful. It established how hard that system is to challenge successfully from inside a single lawsuit, even when the underlying condition being described, an inflexible schedule enforced against a documented medical need, is the exact thing the ADA exists to address.

A separate case has not reached that stage yet. Lashone Brown, a warehouse worker in Las Vegas, was granted official medical leave for surgery to repair two hernias his complaint says he developed on the job. Five days into his approved two-week recovery, Amazon's automated attendance system misclassified his leave as unexcused absence and terminated him. His complaint alleges Amazon's own HR staff acknowledged the error was the company's fault and did not correct it. The case, filed in 2025, is still pending, and nothing here should be read as a verdict on it either way.

Whichever account is more accurate, the direction of the incentive is not in dispute. Documents obtained by The Verge and cited to the National Labor Relations Board showed roughly 300 workers fired at a single Baltimore facility in one year for failing to hit the rate, about ten percent of that site's workforce. In 2021, California passed a law, AB 701, written specifically to force warehouses to disclose these quotas to workers and to stop penalizing time off task taken for health and safety reasons. In 2024, California's Labor Commissioner's Office cited Amazon nearly 5.9 million dollars for violating that same law at two of its distribution warehouses, citing tens of thousands of individual violations. Amazon disputed the findings and appealed the citations, with a company spokesperson stating, "the truth is, we don't have fixed quotas." Disputed or not, a law does not get written for a rare practice, and regulators do not build a case of that size against a company that was never doing the thing the law was written to stop.

Look at what is actually running here, regardless of which account of the last human checkpoint you believe. Definition, invariance, and grading, the same three parts of The Process from the last post, applied to a person instead of a football play. Every task has a standard. The standard does not move. Every attempt gets measured against it. This is what a good method looks like with the caring stripped out. It does not become chaotic. It becomes more efficient, more consistent, and much harder to argue with, because there is far less room left in the loop to argue.

## The current condition

Most workplaces have not gone as far as Amazon. But the direction is not unique to Amazon, and the data on where the broader workforce actually stands says the ordinary version of Scoreboard Leadership is not the exception. It is the norm, and it is getting worse.

Gallup's most recent measurement found that global employee engagement fell to 20 percent in 2025, its lowest level in five years, at a cost of an estimated 10 trillion dollars in lost productivity worldwide, roughly 9 percent of global GDP. It is the second year in a row engagement has dropped, something Gallup had not recorded in over a decade before this. The year before shows the same pattern already underway. Engagement fell from 23 percent in 2023 to 21 percent in 2024, and the drop did not come from individual workers checking out. Individual contributor engagement held close to flat both years. It was managers. Manager engagement has now fallen from 31 percent in 2022 to 22 percent in 2025, the steepest decline of any group Gallup tracks.

The people whose job is to lead others are, as a group, becoming the least engaged people in the building, two years running. The stakes are not abstract. Gallup's own Q12 meta-analysis, spanning over 183,000 business units across 53 industries and 90 countries, found engaged business units run 21 percent more profitable and see meaningfully lower turnover than disengaged ones. Separate research from the Corporate Leadership Council found engaged employees were 87 percent less likely to leave than their disengaged counterparts. A disengaged manager is not a neutral variable sitting off to the side of that outcome. A disengaged manager is the mechanism that produces it downstream, in every person reporting to them.

The mechanism producing that decline is not a mystery, and it is not new to this post. It is the same one running the warehouse floor, moved up a level. A manager scored on personal output while also expected to lead a team is being asked to do two jobs that draw on the same hours. Leading takes time off task by definition, the unscheduled conversation, the person who needs ten minutes before a problem becomes a resignation, the pause required to notice trouble before it shows up in someone else's number. A system that holds a manager to full personal efficiency has built no honest path to success for that manager, because the two things it is asking for cancel each other out. In the language this series has already introduced, that manager's team starts losing Trust first, because consistency of attention is one of the earliest things people notice slipping, and Drift follows close behind it, the gradual separation between what the manager says matters and what the manager actually has time to attend to.

I have written about this exact trade before. In The Producer-Leader Paradox, the argument is that a leader forced to keep producing at full speed loses the capacity to actually lead, because the two draw from the same finite hours. DDI's 2026 Global Leadership Forecast puts numbers on what that produces at scale. Seventy-one percent of leaders report increased stress right now, and forty percent have considered leaving their roles because of it. Only nineteen percent of managers report having strong delegation skills, the one capability that would let a person do both jobs without burning out, and most of them were never given the time to build it in the first place.

## What it costs

Guitron and Ponce de Leon are the answer to a question this piece has not asked directly yet. What happens to the discretionary effort, the honest warning, the willingness to flag a problem before it becomes a scandal, inside a system built entirely around a number. It gets fired. Both women gave Wells Fargo exactly what a healthy organization should want most from the people closest to the work, an early, internal, correctable signal that something was going wrong. The system had no place to put that signal except out the door, because the system was never built to reward anything but the number going up.

Here is the part no scoreboard can show, because it was never built to measure it. Discretionary effort, the extra care, the honest warning, the willingness to stay late without being told, only ever flows toward earned authority. It has never once flowed toward a rate. Wells Fargo could replace 5,300 employees. Amazon can replace the ten percent it loses every year in Baltimore alone. What neither company can buy back is the trust of the employees who stayed, and learned exactly how much the company was willing to sacrifice to hit a number.

This pattern is not contained to the office.

It shows up in a marriage run on the assumption that everything is fine as long as the checks clear. I have heard a wife say the actual sentence out loud: I don't care what he does as long as the checks clear. Provision has replaced partnership as the whole language of care, and both people can point to the bank statement as proof nothing is wrong long after something already is.

It shows up in a friendship that flips to enmity the moment it stops paying out socially. I have lived this one myself. A friendship I trusted turned out to run entirely on what I could provide, introductions, favors, money, and the day I stopped supplying it, the friendship ended with it. I was never his friend. I was his bank, and once the withdrawals stopped, so did the relationship.

It shows up in a parent who measures a child's worth against a path the child never actually chose. It looks like a parent who wanted a doctor or an attorney and got a chef or a musician instead, and started grading the child's life against the credential that never showed up rather than the person who actually did. The relationship narrows to whether the milestones are being hit on schedule, and the child either produces on time or falls short of a scoreboard he never agreed to play on.

None of those relationships announce themselves as transactional. They just quietly start running on a ledger instead of a bond, and the person on the other side of the ledger tends to figure that out long before the one holding the pen does.

## Where this leads

Scoreboard Leadership is not always cruel in intent. Stumpf did not build Eight is Great to hurt anyone. He built it because a number is simpler to manage than a person, easier to defend in a boardroom, easier to point to when investors ask why the stock keeps climbing. A rate does not have a bad week. It does not need a hard conversation. It does not require a leader to sit with someone else's pain long enough to actually understand it. That is exactly what makes it so easy to trust, and exactly why it is not trustworthy at all.

That is why it can win for a while. Wells Fargo posted strong numbers for years before anyone official said the word fraud out loud. Compliance is real and it is fast. What it cannot do is sustain itself, because compliance is the only thing it was ever built to produce, and it runs out the moment the person complying finds a door, or in Wells Fargo's case, the moment enough of them decide fraud is a smaller risk than losing the job.

And it does not end at silence. Silence is the leading indicator, the thing you can hear happening before the real cost shows up. The real cost is a pipeline that stops producing leaders capable of anything but running the scoreboard themselves. Seventy-seven percent of Chief Human Resources Officers say they lack confidence in their bench strength for critical roles, which means the people who would eventually replace a manager burning out under this system are not being developed either, because nobody in the chain has time off task left to develop them. The scoreboard does not just cost the organization the people it grinds down today. It costs the organization the leaders it needed for next year, and the year after that.

Stumpf held the pen for over a decade before the ledger caught up to him. He paid 17.5 million dollars and lost his career and his name in the industry he had spent his whole life inside. Guitron and Ponce de Leon lost their jobs years earlier, for doing the one thing that could have stopped all of it before it reached that scale, and no fine was ever paid to them. Amazon is still holding the pen today. The number always feels safer to the person running it, right up until the moment it fails, and by then the people who could have told him it was failing have already stopped saying anything at all, and the people who could have replaced him were never given the room to become ready.

That collapse, not just the silence, is where Part Three picks up.

docs.title: Use What Was Given
docs.summary: A gift left unused is still a form of unfaithfulness, even when it looks like humility.
docs.email_summary: A gift left unused is still a form of unfaithfulness, even when it looks like humility.
docs.body:
## Scripture

**Romans 12:6–8 (ESV)**

## Reflection

Paul does not describe a single gift distributed evenly. He describes different gifts, given by grace, each with its own manner of use. The list is specific on purpose: teaching is taught, leading is led with zeal, mercy is shown with cheerfulness. Accountability here is not about matching someone else's gift. It is about actually using the one you were given, in the way suited to it.

This is a different kind of accountability than the ones this week has covered so far. It is not about guarding a resource or refusing an unearned privilege. It is about the failure of leaving a genuine gift unused, whether from insecurity, distraction, or simply defaulting to someone else's strengths instead of developing your own.

Leaders are especially prone to this failure with the gift of leading itself. Verse eight names it plainly: the one who leads, with zeal. Not leading tentatively while apologizing for the authority it requires. Not leading by borrowing someone else's style because it looks more comfortable. Leading, as the gift it is, with the energy the gift calls for.

Servant leadership takes accountability for the gift as seriously as it takes accountability for the resource or the title. A leader who has real capacity to lead and exercises it half-heartedly is not being humble. They are letting something they were given by grace go unused, and that is its own form of unfaithfulness.

## Practical Application

- Name your actual gift for leading, teaching, serving, or encouraging, not the gift you wish you had.
- Identify one place you have been using it half-heartedly or borrowing someone else's approach instead.
- Use it fully, in its own manner, this week.

## Takeaways

- Accountability for a gift means actually using it in the way suited to it, not matching someone else's gift.
- A leader with real capacity who exercises it half-heartedly is not being humble; they are letting a gift go unused.

## Closing Thought

A gift left unused is still a form of unfaithfulness, even when it looks like humility.

docs.title: Stewards, Not Owners
docs.summary: What was placed in your care was never yours to begin with, and the accountability follows accordingly.
docs.email_summary: What was placed in your care was never yours to begin with, and the accountability follows accordingly.
docs.body:
## Scripture

**1 Corinthians 4:1–2 (ESV)**

## Reflection

Paul corrects how the Corinthian church has been sizing him up. They had begun ranking leaders against one another, attaching status to whoever they followed. Paul redirects the category entirely. He is not a rival brand of leadership to be preferred over another. He is a steward, managing what belongs to someone else, and the only real measure of a steward is faithfulness.

The word matters because ownership and stewardship produce different kinds of accountability. An owner answers mainly to outcomes they define for themselves. A steward answers to someone else's standard for something that was never theirs to begin with. Paul places every leader, including himself, in the second category.

Leaders slide toward ownership language without noticing. My team. My results. My vision for this organization. None of it is technically false, but all of it can quietly obscure the fact that what a leader manages, whether people, resources, or influence, was placed in their care rather than created by them. Accountability changes shape depending on which category a leader believes they are in.

Servant leadership operates from the steward's position on purpose. The accountability of a steward is not lighter than the accountability of an owner. It may be heavier, because a steward answers not only for results but for how faithfully they managed something that belonged to someone else the entire time.

## Practical Application

- Notice how often you use ownership language for things that were actually entrusted to you.
- Reframe one of them this week in steward's terms: not "my team" but "the team I am accountable for."
- Let that shift change one decision you make this week.

## Takeaways

- An owner answers mainly to outcomes they define; a steward answers to someone else's standard for something that was never theirs.
- The accountability of a steward may be heavier than the accountability of an owner, not lighter.

## Closing Thought

What was placed in your care was never yours to begin with, and the accountability follows accordingly.

docs.title: The Barnabas Archetype
docs.summary: Barnabas gave before proof existed: money, reputation, and a decade of belief in Paul with no contact to back it up. A positive archetype in the leadership series, examined through the same lens as Judas, Absalom, and Nehemiah.
docs.email_summary: Barnabas gave before proof existed: money, reputation, and a decade of belief in Paul with no contact to back it up. A positive archetype in the leadership series, examined through the same lens as Judas, Absalom, and Nehemiah.
docs.body:
His given name was Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus. Somewhere along the way the apostles started calling him something else, and Luke bothers to translate it for us directly in the text: Barnabas, son of encouragement. A nickname that specific does not get attached to a grown man by accident. It gets attached because people watched him do the same thing enough times that his given name stopped being the useful one.

The first thing we see him do earns it. He sold a field he owned and brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet, before anyone was watching closely enough to notice the pattern forming. He did not wait to be asked. He did not wait for a need to be announced publicly. He gave first, quietly, and let the pattern speak for itself. Every story that follows is the same trait applied to people instead of property. Barnabas spends what is his, on other people's behalf, without requiring anything back. That single habit is the whole archetype. It holds through every story that follows, including the one place it breaks.

**The Vouching**

Saul of Tarsus showed up in Jerusalem trying to join the disciples, and the record is blunt about how that went. They were all afraid of him and did not believe he really was a disciple. Reasonably so. This was the man who had been dragging Christians out of their homes. Nobody in that room had a good reason to trust him, and most of them had a personal reason not to.

Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles anyway, and told them how Saul had seen the Lord and preached boldly in Damascus. He put his own standing in that community behind a man whose conversion he could not prove, only describe. He was already established, already trusted, already a name people would send to investigate a report they weren't sure about. He had something real to lose in that room, and he spent it before Paul had done anything to justify the spending. That is the same trait as the field. He gives before the return exists, because the return was never the reason.

**The Decade Nobody Talks About**

Here is the part of the story that gets skipped, and it is the part that proves the pattern held even in silence.

Acts is specific about why Saul, the same man Barnabas had vouched for and who Scripture later calls Paul, left Jerusalem in the first place. The Hellenists there were trying to kill him, and the believers moved him out of the city to keep him alive, sending him first to Caesarea and then home to Tarsus. He was not being reassigned to a new post. He was being hidden.

Working from the chronology in Paul's own letter to the Galatians, most reconstructions place roughly ten years between that departure and the moment Barnabas came looking for him again. Paul himself describes the shape of those years to the Galatians: he was still unknown by face to the churches of Judea, and all they had heard was that the man who once persecuted them was now preaching the faith he had tried to destroy. That is the entire record of a decade. Ten years, and the only line of evidence available is that people who had never met him were relieved they didn't have to.

Barnabas did not spend that decade collecting proof. There is no correspondence in the text, no update, no report confirming Paul had become reliable. When Antioch outgrew what Barnabas could manage alone, he made a hundred-and-fifty-mile trip to bring back a man he had not heard from in ten years, and he was not offering him a quiet role. He was asking Paul to walk back into the kind of visibility that had already nearly gotten him killed once. Barnabas invested in that risk without a shred of new evidence, for the second time, on the same conviction he'd carried the whole decade without needing it renewed. Paul says yes.

**The Reversal He Never Contests**

Barnabas found Paul, brought him back to Antioch, and the two of them spent a full year teaching there together, in the city where believers were first called Christians. Watch what Luke does with their names after that. Early on, the pairing reads "Barnabas and Saul." Barnabas first. He is the senior man, the one Jerusalem trusts enough to send when it needs discernment applied to something uncertain. By the time they are sent out from Antioch on the first missionary expedition, the order in the text has flipped. It is "Paul and Barnabas" from there forward, and nothing in the account shows Barnabas objecting to the change.

That silence is the same trait again, applied to credit instead of money or reputation. He does not need to be seen as the one who made it possible. He built the platform and watched someone else outgrow it, without a recorded word of complaint, because collecting credit was never the point of building it.

**The One Time the Pattern Breaks, and What He Does About It**

Years after Antioch, Paul describes a public confrontation with Peter that scholars now call the Antioch incident, and the stakes were not small. Shared meals between Jewish and Gentile believers were a lived proof of the claim Paul had built his ministry on, that Gentile believers belonged fully without first becoming Jewish. Peter had been eating freely with Gentile believers in Antioch. Then a group arrived from Jerusalem tied to the circumcision party, meaning Jewish Christians who believed Gentile converts still owed circumcision and the law. Under pressure from that group, Peter stopped eating with the Gentile believers and withdrew. That withdrawal reversed, through action, the very inclusion Peter's own life had already testified to. Paul confronted him to his face over it.

Paul's account is direct that Barnabas did not merely witness this. He names him specifically: the rest of the Jews joined Peter in this hypocrisy, and Barnabas was carried along by the same pressure. For the first time in the record, Barnabas protects himself instead of spending himself. He reverses, under social pressure, the same inclusion he had spent years building.

Here is where the archetype either holds or collapses, and this is the detail that decides it. The text does not record Barnabas defending the retreat, explaining it, or staging a visible return to reclaim his standing. It simply shows him, afterward, doing what he always did before the failure: he keeps teaching in Antioch, he stands with Paul at the Jerusalem council defending the same Gentile inclusion he had briefly failed to defend at the table, and when the moment comes to spend himself completely again, he does not hesitate the way he hesitated with Peter. He does not need anyone to watch him make up for Antioch. He simply goes back to giving without requiring anything back, which is the exact same thing he was doing with the field, with Paul, and with his own name. The failure is real and permanent, not erased by what comes after. It does not introduce a second story. It is the clearest proof the first one was real, because a performance of virtue collects credit for its own recovery, and Barnabas never does.

**The Argument He Was Willing to Lose**

Paul and Barnabas planned a second missionary trip, and Barnabas wanted to take John Mark along again. Paul refused, because Mark had deserted them in Pamphylia on the first trip. Luke's description of what followed is spare and exact: there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other.

Barnabas was not asking Paul to ignore what Mark had done. He was applying to Mark the same conviction he had carried through ten silent years with Paul: a person's worst chapter does not have to be the final word. Someone has to stake something real on the second chance before it can exist. He was not trying to win the argument, and he never got proof that his read on Mark was correct. He needed Mark to have the chance, whether or not anyone ever told him giving it was the right call. That is what the disagreement actually cost him. He does not compromise, he does not soften the ask to preserve the partnership, and it costs him the partnership itself. He takes Mark and sails for Cyprus. Luke does not referee who was right. He simply lets Acts continue without Barnabas in it.

**What He Never Gets to Read**

The reconciliation was not a single letter. It was a gradient, visible across years of Paul's own correspondence. Writing to the Corinthians, Paul refers to Barnabas as an active, respected peer still working for a living alongside him. Writing to the Colossians from prison, years later, Paul sends greetings on behalf of Mark, described plainly as the cousin of Barnabas, and instructs the church to welcome him. Only at the very end, in a letter to Timothy written near the close of his own life, does Paul ask for Mark directly, calling him useful to me for ministry. Whatever happened to Mark between the desertion and that final request, it happened because Barnabas kept believing in him after the argument that split two apostles in half.

Barnabas never gets to read that letter. Tradition holds that he and Mark remained together on Cyprus, and that Barnabas was later killed by a mob in Salamis, his body pulled from a fire and buried in secret by Mark. If that account is accurate, the reconciliation he spent his partnership to make possible happened only after he was already gone. He invested completely in an outcome he never collected on, one more time, the same way he had every other time in the story.

**What This Looks Like in a Real Organization**

Branch Rickey spent months building the case before he ever made an offer. Rickey created an elaborate smokescreen to obscure his scouting of Black players, announcing the formation of a new franchise, the Brooklyn Brown Dodgers, and a new Negro League, and dispatching his best talent hunters to observe Black ballplayers, ostensibly for that new franchise but in reality for the Dodgers. He built an entire false organization as cover before he ever sat Robinson down.

When the two men finally met, it wasn't a handshake and a contract. Rickey wanted to see if Robinson had the courage and self-control to handle what the first Black player would endure, and after three hours of probing, personal questions, and role-playing confrontations, Robinson left the office with the promise of a contract. Rickey had already tried this approach once and walked away. In 1945, Rickey met with Cuban player Silvio García and asked him what he would do if a white American slapped his face; García answered that he would kill him, and he was not signed. The bet wasn't just on talent. It was on a specific kind of restraint Rickey had already watched fail once in someone else.

The cost was not abstract or momentary. Rickey was called "The Mahatma" or "El Cheapo," depending on who was writing about him, and after signing Robinson he was both praised and damned at the same time, with no in-between. A columnist at the New York Daily News made a habit of attacking him over it, and by his own account, it got so bad that in 1946 Rickey considered suing over it. He carried that reputational cost personally, in the press, for years, not as a single bad news cycle he weathered and moved past.

And the spending did not stop at the signing. Rickey's support stayed steady over the next five years: he helped stifle a clubhouse revolt before Robinson was promoted to the Dodgers in 1947, stood with him in racist confrontations with the Phillies and Cardinals, and insisted Robinson would play in Southern exhibition games, notably in Atlanta in 1949. That last detail matters. Rickey did not wait for the pressure to ease before pushing Robinson into more of it. He kept spending his own standing on Robinson's inclusion for half a decade, past the point where the initial risk had already proven itself.

**The Actual Archetype**

Set beside the others in this series, Barnabas belongs with Joseph and Nehemiah, not with Judas, Absalom, and Saul.

Judas took, quietly, while performing devotion out loud. Absalom built a following by locating a real grievance and standing inside it for his own gain. Saul was chosen and given every advantage a leader could ask for, and his fall came from what he chose to protect once he finally had power. Different triggers, greed, grievance, position, but the same direction. Each of them spent what they had on themselves, and the pattern only hardens as their stories continue.

Joseph absorbed betrayal and kept serving faithfully in a prison cell with no promise of release. Nehemiah rebuilt a wall while holding off external threats and corruption inside his own community at the same time, without letting either one go unanswered. Barnabas gives before proof exists, releases credit without contest, and returns to giving after his own failure without needing anyone to notice the return. Three different forms of the same trait.

None of the three got to see the full return on what they gave. Joseph didn't know if the prison would end. Nehemiah didn't get a guarantee the wall would hold once he was gone. Barnabas didn't live to learn if Mark was worth what the partnership cost him. That absence of a guaranteed payoff is not a detail of their stories. It's the actual test. Self-interested leadership needs the ledger to close in its favor before it will give anything at all. Servant leadership gives before the ledger closes, and sometimes before it ever closes at all.

**The Question This Archetype Asks**

Every leader has made at least one decision that required believing in someone before the evidence existed. Fewer have made a habit of it, in money, in credit, and in the people everyone else had already written off. Fewer still have applied that same habit to their own worst moment, choosing to quietly return to the pattern instead of staging a comeback that required an audience.

Barnabas never found out if Mark was worth it. He built a case for Paul that he wouldn't see settled for a decade, released a title without a fight, failed once under pressure and repaired it without asking to be forgiven out loud, then spent his last partnership on a second chance he never lived to see justified. None of it came back to him. That is not the cost of this archetype. That is the archetype.

docs.title: The Governor Who Refused the Allowance
docs.summary: The accountability that matters most is the kind no one is checking but you.
docs.email_summary: The accountability that matters most is the kind no one is checking but you.
docs.body:
## Scripture

**Nehemiah 5:14–15 (ESV)**

## Reflection

Nehemiah had a legal right to the governor's allowance. Every governor before him had taken it, some heavily. No one would have questioned him for doing what every predecessor had done. He refused it anyway, for twelve years, and names the reason plainly: the fear of God.

This is accountability practiced where no external accountability existed. Nehemiah answered to the king who appointed him and, in a sense, to the people he governed, but neither was tracking the food allowance he was legally entitled to claim. The only accountability actively operating in that decision was the one Nehemiah imposed on himself.

Leaders inherit privileges the same way Nehemiah inherited the governor's allowance: as standard practice, defensible by precedent, unlikely to be challenged. What previous leaders took, current leaders can usually take too, without anyone raising an objection. Precedent quietly becomes permission, and permission quietly becomes an excuse to stop asking whether something is right.

Servant leadership treats personal accountability as active even when external accountability has gone silent. Nehemiah did not wait for someone to question the allowance before deciding not to take it. He held himself to a standard higher than the one he had inherited, not because the position demanded it, but because he refused to let his position be the only thing measuring his conduct.

## Practical Application

- Identify one privilege in your role that came to you by precedent rather than by anyone actively deciding it was right.
- Ask whether you would still take it if you had to justify it from scratch.
- Set it aside, or reduce it, if the honest answer is no.

## Takeaways

- Nehemiah practiced accountability where no external accountability was tracking him.
- Precedent quietly becomes permission, and permission quietly becomes an excuse to stop asking whether something is right.

## Closing Thought

The accountability that matters most is the kind no one is checking but you.

docs.body:
## Scripture

**Luke 19:15–19 (ESV)**

## Reflection

Before the nobleman leaves to receive his kingdom, he hands each servant a mina and gives a single instruction: engage in business until I come back. When he returns, he does not ask what they preserved. He asks what they produced. The account he settles is a record of activity, not a record of safekeeping.

This distinction matters for how leaders think about accountability. It is easy to treat accountability as a defensive posture, something you satisfy by not losing what was given to you. Nothing broken, nothing missing, nothing to explain. The servants in this parable are not commended for avoiding loss. They are commended for what the entrusted resource became in their hands.

Leadership often narrows accountability down to risk management, holding steady, not being the one who caused the problem. That is real accountability, but it is not the whole of it. Genuine accountability for what a leader has been given includes what they did with it, not only what they protected it from.

Servant leadership settles its own account the way these servants did, by measuring what was made of what was entrusted. A leader who can say only that nothing was lost has met a lower bar than this parable sets. The full account includes growth, not just preservation.

## Practical Application

- List what has been entrusted to your leadership: budget, people, time, authority.
- For each one, ask whether you have merely preserved it or actually put it to work.
- Choose one area where preservation has quietly replaced production, and change that this month.

## Takeaways

- The account settled in this parable is a record of activity, not a record of safekeeping.
- A leader who can say only that nothing was lost has met a lower bar than full accountability requires.

## Closing Thought

Accountability for what you were given includes what you built with it, not only what you protected.

docs.summary: What was given in trust is what will be required in full.
docs.email_summary: What was given in trust is what will be required in full.
docs.body:
## Scripture

**Luke 12:47–48 (ESV)**

## Reflection

Jesus closes this teaching on the faithful and unwise manager with a principle that scales rather than a rule that applies evenly. Two servants fail. Both are held accountable. But the servant who knew more carries a heavier accountability than the one who did not, because the measure of accountability is tied to what was entrusted, not just to what went wrong.

Leaders rarely think of authority this way. Authority tends to feel like a reward, a mark of trust earned, a wider platform to build from. It is also a wider account to answer for. The leader with more reach, more resources, more people depending on their decisions, is not simply more capable. They are more accountable, whether they have thought about it in those terms or not.

This is uncomfortable in a specific way. It means accountability is not a fixed standard applied equally to everyone in a room. It moves with authority. The leader with the most influence in an organization carries the most accountability in that organization, even when no one has said so out loud.

Servant leadership treats increasing responsibility as increasing accountability, not increasing exemption. The temptation as a leader gains more is to assume more latitude, more benefit of the doubt, more distance from the consequences other people face. This verse reverses that assumption entirely. What was given in trust is what will be required in full.

## Practical Application

- Name one area where your authority has grown faster than your sense of accountability for it.
- Ask what standard you would hold someone else to if they had exactly what you have been given.
- Hold yourself to that same standard starting this week.

## Takeaways

- The measure of accountability is tied to what was entrusted, not just to what went wrong.
- Increasing responsibility means increasing accountability, not increasing exemption.

## Closing Thought

What was given in trust is what will be required in full.

docs.title: Each Will Give Account
docs.summary: Accountability owed for one's self is a debt no amount of leadership can transfer.
docs.email_summary: Accountability owed for one's self is a debt no amount of leadership can transfer.
docs.body:
## Scripture

**Romans 14:10–12 (ESV)**

## Reflection

Paul has spent this section of Romans addressing believers who were quick to judge one another over disputable matters, what to eat, which days to observe. Before he tells them to stop, he reminds them why the judging was never theirs to do. Everyone will stand before the judgment seat of God. Each will give an account of himself.

That last phrase is the turn. Not an account of someone else. Not an account of a team, a decision made by committee, or a culture a leader inherited. An account of himself. The accountability Paul describes cannot be delegated, shared, or diffused across an organization chart.

Leaders spend most of their working lives managing collective accountability, whose team missed the target, which department owns the failure, how responsibility gets distributed fairly across a group. That work matters. But underneath it sits a category of accountability that never becomes collective. What a leader personally chose to believe, to overlook, to excuse in themselves, remains theirs alone to answer for.

Servant leadership holds both categories without confusing them. A leader is accountable for the people and outcomes entrusted to them, and separately, irreducibly, accountable for who they personally were inside every one of those decisions. The second kind cannot be satisfied by pointing to the first. No amount of organizational success covers a personal account left unexamined.

Paul's conclusion, that each of us will give an account of himself to God, is not a threat aimed at silencing the judgmental believers he was correcting. It is the reason judging others was always beside the point. Everyone carries a full account of their own that no one else can carry for them.

## Practical Application

- Separate your accountability for outcomes your team owns from your accountability for choices only you made.
- Identify one personal choice this month you have been folding into a team's collective result instead of owning directly.
- Give yourself the same honest account you would expect from someone reporting to you.

## Takeaways

- The accountability Paul describes cannot be delegated, shared, or diffused across an organization chart.
- No amount of organizational success covers a personal account left unexamined.

## Closing Thought

Accountability owed for one's self is a debt no amount of leadership can transfer.

docs.title: Nothing Stays Hidden
docs.summary: Accountability that exists only in public is not accountability at all.
docs.email_summary: Accountability that exists only in public is not accountability at all.
docs.body:
## Scripture

**Luke 12:2–3 (ESV)**

## Reflection

Jesus is not describing a distant future event. He is describing how concealment actually works. What is covered gets uncovered. What is whispered gets repeated somewhere louder than it was said.

Leaders often treat private conversations as a separate category from public leadership, as though what is said behind closed doors carries different weight than what is said from the front of the room. This passage removes that distinction entirely.

The private comment about a struggling team member. The frustrated aside about a decision the leader disagreed with in public. The conversation held in confidence that was never actually meant to stay there. All of it eventually surfaces in some form, whether through a person repeating it or through the leader's own pattern becoming visible over time.

Servant leadership treats the private and the public as the same territory of accountability, governed by the same standard. A leader who says one thing in the boardroom and something different in the hallway is not managing two audiences well. They are building a gap in their own accountability that will eventually close on its own, usually at a cost the leader did not choose.

The instruction here is not to say less. It is to hold the same accountability regardless of who is in the room.

## Practical Application

- Compare what you say about a decision privately to what you say about it publicly.
- Close any gap you find between the two versions.
- Speak about people the same way whether they are present or not.

## Takeaways

- What is said privately eventually surfaces, and accountability does not distinguish between the two audiences.
- A leader who says one thing privately and another publicly is building a gap in their own accountability.

## Closing Thought

Accountability that exists only in public is not accountability at all.

docs.title: Our Secret Sins in the Light
docs.summary: Accountability for a leader's private decisions does not wait for a public moment.
docs.email_summary: Accountability for a leader's private decisions does not wait for a public moment.
docs.body:
## Scripture

**Psalm 90:8 (ESV)**

## Reflection

Moses writes this psalm near the end of a life spent leading people who resisted him constantly. He knows what it is to carry decisions no one else saw him make.

The verse does not describe a future exposure. It describes a present condition. The secret sins are already in the light of God's presence. Accountability for a leader's private decisions does not wait for a public moment. It is already in effect.

This is uncomfortable for a reason. Leaders operate with more unseen latitude than almost anyone else in an organization. Fewer people are positioned to question a leader's choices in the moment they are made. That latitude can become a private category of decisions a leader assumes will never be accountable to anyone.

Servant leadership does not rely on the assumption of privacy to behave well. Accountability that only holds when someone is watching is not accountability. It is performance. Assuming every decision is already known, seen or unseen, changes what a leader is willing to do when no one else is positioned to ask.

The leaders who hold up over time are rarely the ones who never had a hidden option available. They are the ones who stopped believing hidden options were exempt from accountability.

## Practical Application

- Identify one decision you have made recently that you assumed no one would examine closely.
- Evaluate it as though it were already visible to everyone you lead.
- Adjust anything that only survives scrutiny because it has avoided it so far.

## Takeaways

- Accountability for a leader's private decisions does not wait for a public moment.
- The leaders who hold up over time are the ones who stopped believing hidden options were exempt from accountability.

## Closing Thought

What feels unseen is simply unexamined, not unaccountable.

docs.title: They Still Call Him
docs.summary: Part one of a five-part series on transformational and servant leadership. Nick Saban's 1998 phone call to a stranger, days before the biggest game of his career, is the proof that transactional leadership fails under real pressure and what has to replace it.
docs.email_summary: Part one of a five-part series on transformational and servant leadership. Nick Saban's 1998 phone call to a stranger, days before the biggest game of his career, is the proof that transactional leadership fails under real pressure and what has to replace it.
docs.body:
# They Still Call Him

*Part One of a series on transformational and servant leadership*

Transformational leadership is the mode. Servant leadership is the account it draws on.

Five posts make this argument in full. Here we start with the method, and what has to sit underneath it for the method to mean anything. Next comes the operating system most organizations are actually running, the one that takes a good set of habits and points them at the wrong thing. After that, what it looks like when a high-demand team holds a real standard and keeps its people safe at the same time. Then the account gets tested under fire, in the one setting where nobody has time to explain anything and trust is the only thing that moves people. And last, your Tuesday. Almost nobody reading this coaches football, at least not on Saturday in front of 100,000 people. On Tuesday you lead your own team, and you've been the underdog for years.

In 1998 Nick Saban was the head coach at Michigan State and his team was headed to Columbus to play the number one team in the country. Ohio State was undefeated and had been dismantling people. Nobody outside that locker room gave Michigan State a chance.

Saban did not give them one either. He has said so himself. That was the real problem. He did not know how to coach a team without making the win the point, and it had nothing to do with the players in that locker room.

He was a transactional coach at that point in his career. Do the work, get the result, answer for it when you miss. That system had carried him from a small town in West Virginia to a Big Ten head coaching job, and it failed him in the week he needed it most. A coach cannot sell a win he does not believe in. Players read their coach faster than they read a game plan, and they were going to hear what he actually thought no matter what came out of his mouth on Thursday.

So he picked up the phone and called a psychiatrist named Lonny Rosen who taught at Michigan State.

I want to step back here, because this next part teaches something different than the rest of the story. A man near the top of his profession, days out from the biggest game of his career, called a stranger and admitted he did not know how to lead the team in front of him. Most leaders in that position give a speech instead. It costs nothing. It also fixes nothing, and everyone in the room can tell.

Rosen did not offer motivation. He came at it from performance psychology, where the central finding is unglamorous. Focusing on an outcome you cannot control produces anxiety, and anxiety degrades the execution that would have produced the outcome. Wanting it more makes it worse.

A football play lasts about four to six seconds. A game holds sixty or seventy of them. Rosen told him to stop coaching the game and coach the play. Line up, execute your assignment at the highest level you are capable of, let it go, and do it again.

Michigan State won 28 to 24.

Forget the score. A team full of nineteen year olds walked into the most hostile building in the country against the best team in the country and did not fold, because somebody had finally given them a way to succeed that had nothing to do with the scoreboard. Do this one assignment right, for four to six seconds, and you have already won, whatever the drive does next. Stack enough of those up and you might just beat the number one team in the country.

## What The Process actually is

That week became the seed. Over the next twenty five years Saban built it into something he eventually called The Process, and it went well past a mental trick. It has three parts and they hold each other up.

The first is definition. Every task has a correct way to perform it, and that way gets written down and taught. Not the goal. The method. Where the eyes go on the snap. What the hands do. What the first step looks like. A standard nobody can picture is not a standard, it is a wish, and most organizations are full of them.

The second is invariance. The standard does not move for the opponent, the score, the weather, or the week. A player who goes all out against a ranked team and coasts against a weak one has not met the standard. He has met the situation. Saban calls situational effort the primary disease in talented people. It wins often enough to feel like success. Underneath, it teaches an entire team that effort is negotiable, and once that lesson lands you cannot unteach it with a speech.

The third is grading. Every attempt gets measured against the definition instead of against whether it worked. A play can gain fifteen yards and grade out as a failure, because the assignment was blown and the result was luck. A play can lose four yards and grade out clean. Across a season that separates execution from fortune, and separating those two is the only way anyone learns anything from a result.

Here is the gift buried in that third part, and it is not a secret worth hiding. Outcome-based measurement guarantees that most people fail most of the time no matter what they do, because outcomes are contaminated by things nobody controls. The economy. The competitor. The client who reorganized. Execution-based measurement means effort always converts. Saban gave those kids a definition of success they could hit one hundred percent of the time, on the worst day, in a game they were going to lose.

Four years of that changes a person. He learns that his effort is real currency. He learns that the standard is not a lottery. He learns that showing up fully is never wasted, even when the scoreboard says otherwise. Then he graduates and carries it into a marriage, a business, a diagnosis, a bad year.

That is not a football lesson.

## A method is not a purpose

This is what I mean by method, and it is what I will mean every time I use the word from here forward. A method answers how. How do we practice, how do we measure, how do we hold a line. The Process, with its three parts, is a method. A purpose answers what for, and underneath that, what we owe the people doing the work. A method can be attached to any purpose you want, good or bad, because a method by itself has no opinion about what it is for.

That is not a criticism of it. Methods are supposed to be silent about purpose. The trouble starts when a leader mistakes his method for his ethic and decides that because his system is rigorous, his intentions must be sound. Rigor is not evidence of anything except rigor.

Any organization can install The Process tomorrow. Define every task. Hold the standard in every condition. Grade every attempt. Plenty of companies already run a version of this on their own people, keystroke tracking, call-time quotas, activity dashboards that log every minute of a workday. Definition, invariance, and grading, aimed at a person instead of a task. If the organization already treats people as inputs, none of that corrects anything. It makes the extraction more precise, better documented, and much harder to argue with.

I have spent a couple of years researching and writing about that failure mode. I call it Scoreboard Leadership, a term I coined and own the domain for, and it is the subject of the next post in this series. For now it is enough to say that it is transactional at the foundation, that the number becomes the mission, and that handing it a method as good as Saban's makes it sharper rather than better.

So The Process by itself never explains Saban. Definition, invariance, and grading run inside plenty of organizations that produce nothing but throughput and turnover. Something else was underneath his, something no method, by itself, can supply.

## What Burns had and Bass removed

The words we use for what Saban did come from two men, and the gap between them is the argument.

James MacGregor Burns was a political scientist and a presidential historian. In 1978 he published a book called Leadership, and in it he drew a line between transactional leadership, which runs on exchange, and what he called transforming leadership, where leader and follower raise each other to higher levels of motivation and morality.

Burns built morality into the definition itself. In his framing, you could not be a transforming leader while degrading the people you led. It did not matter what they achieved. Achievement was not the test.

Bernard Bass was an organizational psychologist at Binghamton. In 1985 he moved the idea out of politics and into companies, and he built an instrument to measure it. He named four components. Model something worth following. Articulate a vision that lifts people. Challenge them to think. Attend to each person individually. The instrument made the concept usable, and it is the only reason the term exists in business at all.

To make it measurable, he took the morality out. Bass argued that a leader could be transformational regardless of the ends being served. For years that was the accepted position, and business kept producing the cases that proved it couldn't hold. Elizabeth Holmes built Theranos on a real vision, real charisma, and total devotion from employees who believed they were about to change medicine. The technology never worked, and people got hurt trusting it. Adam Neumann built WeWork on the same fuel, a mission bigger than a real estate company, employees who would have followed him anywhere, and it ended in a collapse that cost thousands of them their jobs and their equity. Both men were transformational by Bass's 1985 definition. Neither one had the morality Burns had built in seven years earlier. By 1999 Bass was bolting a distinction back on, separating authentic transformational leaders from what he called pseudo-transformational ones. The difference in his own definition came down to intent and ethical impact. A pseudo-transformational leader shows every behavior on the checklist and still leaves people worse off, because none of it was ever in service of them. That is a careful way of admitting the original definition had been right and the measurable version had a hole in it.

Put the morality back and the two descriptions collapse into one. A leader who raises people to higher levels of motivation and morality, and who will not degrade them on the way, is a servant leader operating under high demand.

So when I say transformational leadership and servant leadership are closer than anyone gives them credit for, I am not proposing something new. I am pointing at what got removed so the idea would fit on a questionnaire.

## They knew what they signed up for

Saban's players opted into hard. Every one of them had spent ten years becoming the kind of athlete a program like that would take. They had already lined up against the kids who ended up at Ohio State. Nobody arrived in Tuscaloosa confused about what the standard would be. That was the whole appeal of the place.

When Saban demanded more than they thought they had in them, he was not imposing a cost on them. He was delivering the thing they came for.

Servant leadership was never about comfort. Lowering the bar for someone who came to be forged is not kindness. It is a betrayal with better manners. Good players get cut every year for missing an agreed upon mark, and that is not a failure of service. It is the agreement working.

But an agreement is not a slogan on a wall. A real one has three parts. Everyone knows what the standard is. Everyone knows why it exists and what it protects. And everyone had a genuine choice about whether to be there. Take away any one of those three and what is left is not an agreement. It is a demand dressed up to look like one.

The high performance environment is not where servant leadership gets diluted. It is the only place you can actually see it. In a low demand room, a servant leader is indistinguishable from a merely pleasant one. Turn the pressure up and the difference becomes the only thing that matters.

## The leader you actually had

Somewhere behind you is the most demanding person you ever worked for. The one with the impossible standard. The one who made you redo it. The one whose approval you can still feel the shape of, years later.

If you had a problem tomorrow that person could help with, would you still call them?

Hold that question, because the answer depends on which of three people you actually had.

One ran you on a trade. Show up, produce, collect the paycheck. His approval was never really available. What you got was the appearance of it, and only for as long as the numbers held.

One pushed you further than you thought you had in you and got the result, whatever it cost you to give it to him. He was not lying to you. He also was not thinking about you once he had what he needed.

And one did both at the same time. Same demand, same standard, same redo. Underneath all of it, he was for you.

The demand looked identical in all three. The hours were identical. The standard was identical. From the outside, on any given Tuesday, you could not have told them apart.

The difference was never the intensity. It was the care. That is servant leadership showing up inside transformational leadership, which is exactly how Burns mapped it in 1978 before Bass took the morality out to make it measurable. Take the care out and you still get results. You just don't get someone you would call ten years later with a problem that has nothing to do with what he once demanded of you.

That is the gap between a method and a purpose, and you have been carrying the evidence for it your entire working life.

## He left because he cared

That gap is what makes sense of Saban walking away, and it is worth saying plainly before the story runs. He left because the thing he cared about most had been taken out of the job. Not the winning. The other thing.

In January 2024 he walked away from Alabama at seventy-two, coming off a season where he believed the next team was going to be very good. He was not fired. He was not losing. He left.

Speaking on Capitol Hill that March, he said that everything he had believed in across fifty years of coaching no longer existed in college athletics, and that it had always been about developing players and helping people become more successful in life.

He told ESPN that seventy or eighty percent of the players he talked to in those final weeks wanted to know two things. Whether they were guaranteed to play, and how much he would pay them. He said the program had always been built on how much value it could create for a young man's future, through personal development, academic success, and preparation for a career. He was careful to add that he did not think the players were wrong to want what they wanted. Only that it had never been what his program was about, and never why it had worked.

Miss Terry probably knew it before he did. That is what everyone calls Nick's wife of more than fifty years, and she has never been a coach's wife standing off to the side. Every account of their life together describes the same thing from a different angle: she was the one who noticed what a player needed before he asked, who built relationships behind the ones Nick got credit for, who understood the players were never just athletes to either of them. She helped build the heart of that program as much as he did.

Whatever the two of them worked out between themselves in those final months, the deal on the table had changed. These players were not signing up to be developed into men anymore. Most of them were signing up to get paid to play college football for a year, then leave for a bigger number somewhere else. The relationship an eighteen year old walked into ten years earlier was not the relationship walking through the door now, no matter how badly Nick and Miss Terry wanted it to be.

His age was part of it too, and he has said so. Hiring the staff he needed and holding the standard at the level he was used to had both gotten harder. That is real, and it does not compete with the other reason. It sits beside it.

He could still recruit a roster. He could still win with it. What he could no longer do was spend four years turning a young man into someone who would still be that person twenty years later. That was gone before he ever decided to leave. Retiring was him admitting it out loud.

What was left was paying for wins.

That is a transaction. Nothing more. And it is exactly what he had walked away from in 1998, when he called a stranger and admitted the transactional version of himself could not get his team through Saturday.

Twenty six years later the transaction came back and took the job. So he left it.

## Proof, not performance

Saban did not have to prove any of this. He is one of the winningest coaches who has ever lived, financially secure, retired, and he owes nothing else to anyone. There was no audience left for him to perform for. Which is exactly why what comes next is the real evidence, not a reason to doubt what already happened.

Anyone can look caring while people are still deciding whether to work for him. The only place a leader cannot fake it is after he no longer needs anything from the people in question.

They still call him.

Twenty years out. Careers over. Rings in a drawer somewhere. Nothing left for either party to gain. Saban is documented checking on former players long after they left Tuscaloosa, walking them through personal trouble and connecting them to work.

He also rebuilt coaching careers nobody else would touch. Steve Sarkisian came to him after a public collapse. Mike Locksley came to him after a run at New Mexico that should have ended him. Neither man could do a thing for Saban at the moment he took him on. Sarkisian has since described a person the public never sees and called him one of the most compassionate people he has been around, and then pointed out that this is not how anybody describes him.

The test is simple and almost nobody passes it. What does a leader do for a person who can no longer produce?

The extractive version reallocates. There is nothing personal in it. The math simply stops working and the resources go elsewhere. The servant keeps investing in someone who is now pure cost, and gets nothing measurable back for it. That does not mean the investment is endless or unconditional. It means it is not billed by the hour, and it does not stop the day the usefulness does.

On the practice field those two men are identical. Same standard, same intensity, same conversation with the same kid about the same missed assignment. You cannot tell them apart while it is happening.

Ten years later they are not remotely the same, and by then everybody knows which one they had.

Nick Saban cared about those men more than he cared about winning. Not instead of winning. He is the most relentless winner the sport has produced and he never pretended otherwise. More than. And the one time the two came apart, when the system finally made him choose between developing people and collecting trophies, he put down the best job in college football and walked out of the building.

## Where this series goes

Transformational leadership is the mode. Servant leadership is the account it draws on.

The Process is a method, and a good one, and it explains none of what made Nick Saban the greatest builder of men college football has produced. What explains it is that he cared about those players as students and as men before he cared about what they did on Saturday. They knew it. And they gave him everything on the strength of it.

Not because caring is the nicer road to the same destination. Because anyone can extract for four years. Sustaining excellence for twenty five requires discretionary effort, the effort nobody can compel or measure or write into a contract, and discretionary effort only ever flows toward earned authority.

Scoreboard Leadership comes next, and it does not stay inside the office. It follows people home, into marriages, friendships, and the way a father talks to a son.

After that, what a high-demand team looks like when the standard is real and the people are safe at the same time, and what it costs a leader to build one.

The account gets tested under fire in the post after that. The one condition where nobody has time to explain anything and trust is the only thing that moves people.

And last, your Tuesday. Almost nobody reading this coaches football. At least not on Saturday, in front of 100,000 people. On Tuesday you lead your team, and you have been twenty-point underdogs for years.

If you grow people, you grow the organization. If you use people, you lose it.

Roll Tide.

docs.title: Achan's Confession
docs.summary: Accountability offered before it is demanded is what makes an account trustworthy.
docs.email_summary: Accountability offered before it is demanded is what makes an account trustworthy.
docs.body:
## Scripture

**Joshua 7:19–21 (ESV)**

## Reflection

Joshua does not open with an accusation. He asks Achan to give glory to God and to tell the truth. The invitation comes before the confrontation.

Achan's answer is immediate and complete. He does not minimize what he took. He does not explain it away as a misunderstanding. He names what he saw, what he wanted, what he did, and where he hid it.

Leaders rarely get a confession this clean, and rarely give one either. The instinct under pressure is to soften the account, to leave out the detail that makes it worse, to explain the decision in a way that sounds more reasonable than it was. Achan does none of that. He treats accountability as complete, not partial.

Servant leadership depends on this kind of complete accountability, not partial honesty dressed up to look complete. A leader who admits fault but withholds the specifics that make it costly has not actually been accountable. They have managed the story. The difference matters to the people who have to trust the account they are given.

What makes Achan's confession significant is not that consequences followed. It is that he offered accountability before being shown the evidence. Joshua asked, and Achan answered fully, without negotiating the terms of his own admission.

## Practical Application

- The next time you have to admit a mistake, include the specific details, not just the general shape of it.
- Resist the urge to explain your way into a better version of what happened.
- Give the complete account before someone else has to extract it from you.

## Takeaways

- A leader who admits fault but withholds the specifics has not actually been accountable. They have managed the story.
- Accountability offered before it is demanded is what makes an account trustworthy.

## Closing Thought

Accountability given freely carries more weight than accountability extracted under pressure.

docs.title: Be Sure Your Sin Will Find You Out
docs.summary: Accountability does not stay quiet. It surfaces in the record of what a leader actually did.
docs.email_summary: Accountability does not stay quiet. It surfaces in the record of what a leader actually did.
docs.body:
## Scripture

**Numbers 32:20–23 (ESV)**

## Reflection

Moses lays out the agreement in full before naming the warning. Reuben and Gad may settle east of the Jordan on one condition, cross over armed, fight alongside the rest of Israel until the land is subdued, then return home free of the obligation. The warning in verse twenty-three only makes sense against that condition. If they do not follow through, failure to keep the commitment becomes sin against the LORD, and sin that will not stay hidden.

The warning is not about getting caught in a legal sense. It is about the nature of accountability itself. Commitments do not stay quiet. They surface in the record of what a person actually did, regardless of what was promised.

Leaders make commitments constantly, to teams, to boards, to customers, to their own stated values. Most of those commitments are made in rooms where enforcement is loose and memory is short. That looseness is exactly what makes this verse relevant. The absence of an immediate consequence does not mean accountability was forgotten.

Servant leadership treats every commitment as a matter of accountability, not just intention. It assumes the account will eventually be checked, because it will. People remember what a leader promised, even after the leader has moved on to the next initiative. What was promised and what was delivered rarely stay separate for long. Accountability closes that distance whether a leader tracks it or not.

This is not a reason to make fewer promises. It is a reason to hold every promise to the same accountability. A leader who says less and follows through completely builds something sturdier than a leader who says more and lets half of it quietly disappear.

## Practical Application

- List the commitments you have made in the last month that are still outstanding.
- Identify which ones you have quietly hoped no one would remember.
- Follow through on one this week without being reminded.

## Takeaways

- Accountability does not stay quiet. It surfaces in the record of what a leader actually did.
- A leader who says less and follows through completely builds more trust than one who promises more and delivers less.

## Closing Thought

Accountability does not require a reminder. It only requires time.

docs.title: The Absalom Archetype
docs.summary: Absalom never accused David of failing. He just stood in a gap his father left open, morning after morning, until the sympathy he built there cost David his own most trusted counselor.
docs.email_summary: Absalom never accused David of failing. He just stood in a gap his father left open, morning after morning, until the sympathy he built there cost David his own most trusted counselor.
docs.body:
# The Absalom Archetype
*The Archetype Series, Entry Five*

---
