docs.body:
A quick update and two ideas worth more than an update episode usually delivers.

The show is coming back. Technical issues with the production system are behind me and it is time to start moving again. Guest episodes begin August 6th. I am also bringing in a friend, Michael Corcoran, a veteran video producer and interviewer, to run a new interview format starting the week of August 10th. Target is eight to ten episodes recorded in that format. The monologue format has been more challenging than I want it to be and it has been slowing down content that I think can help people. This is the fix.

I have been doing a deep dive into transformational leadership and how closely it aligns with servant leadership. Nick Saban is the vessel for this story. He was coaching Michigan State in 1998, twenty point underdogs going into number one Ohio State, and he knew he could not coach them to win that game as a transactional leader. So he called a psychiatrist on campus. The conversation shifted everything. Stop chasing the outcome. Coach the play. Every play lasts four to six seconds. There are fifty to seventy of them in a game. If you invest in the people executing each one, the leadership you put into them carries them forward whether they win the play or not. Michigan State won by four points. What I learned researching this is that transformational leadership and servant leadership are far more compatible than I expected. The piece that connects them is care. His players still call him today, guys who won championships fifteen and twenty five years ago. That tells me everything. Five to seven posts coming in a new journal series.

I have also never made a single decision in my life without accountability. Not one. I meet with six to eight people regularly and I still feel like an imposter despite the track record. The same input consistently over time generates the same output. If you want a different output you have to change the input. The August devotional series is built around accountability and it is almost ready.

The Archetype Series is live. Judas, Joseph, Saul, and Nehemiah at archetypeoriginal.com. Biblical leaders examined as real leadership case studies, not sermon material.
docs.transcript:
Bart Paden (00:09)
Hey there, it's Bart. This is maybe an update for the Archetype Original Podcast. I owe you guys some information. over the last couple of weeks I've run into some technical difficulties with the system that I built to help me produce the show and and get it hosted and put in places where you guys can find it. so I took a beat here and and got my stuff together and it's almost there.

And I feel pretty confident in how it is going. So it's time to start recording again, and I wanted to also give you an update there on what's going on. I've got some guest episodes that I'm beginning to schedule that will begin next week. I think my first recording is August 6th. Hope to have that episode turned around really, really quickly so we can start getting this going again.

And then I've also brought in a friend of mine, Michael Corcoran, who is a video producer. Who has a lot of experience interviewing and asking questions and he's helped me with things for a lot of years. And he's gonna do some interviewing me because I do know that I have had some good success in interviews. I feel like things go better for me there and this monologue stuff is just more challenging than I want it to be. It's actually preventing me from getting content out there that I think will help you guys. So we're gonna make a shift.

And we'll start recording those the week of August tenth. our target is eight to ten episodes that will get recorded that I can present to you all in that format. So hopefully that helps. Couple of updates. I've been working really hard on this archetype series, looking at all of the people right now that are biblical characters. if you've read the Bible or been close to it at all, there's a lot of people in there that lead and there's good leaders and bad leaders. I started with Judas. I went to Joseph. I did Saul and those three blog posts are out there right now and are available to read. I think they're really helpful for anybody who reads them.

It's not just preaching and sermon stuff, it's legitimately connecting things that are part of a really important book, however you perceive it, that talk about how people lead and the consequences of those actions. So I think it's something that's definitely worth checking out. I'm also working on a new podcast or not podcasts, a new journal series.

I posted a video just a few days ago with Nick Saban sharing a transformation that he went through back in the late 90s from transactional leadership to transformational leadership. And I started researching how that connects to servant leadership, which is the model that I really believe in and I'm trying to build this business around. And it's been really, really interesting to me. and some of the things that that I'm researching in it are not just football related, but leadership related, of course. And the idea of transactional leadership where effectively somebody has something that you want and as long as they are doing the thing they in the way that you want them to do it, everything's fine. And I've experienced a lot of that in my career in so many different forms. and I'm sure you guys have too if if we're being honest.

And I just don't think it's healthy. But Nick talked about he was coaching Michigan State at the time. They were getting ready to go play Ohio State. they were twenty point underdogs. Ohio State was number one in the country. And Nick knew that his team couldn't win that game. There was no way he could coach them to win that game. He didn't understand how, and it was because he was a transactional leader.

And if you can't get the outcome that you want, it's almost impossible to coach a team. You can't lead very well if you don't as a transactional leader if you don't know the outcome, if you can't get there. it becomes really, really challenging to lead in that way. so he picked up the phone and he called a psychiatrist that worked on campus for Michigan State. And the guy, and I have his name in the post that you'll be able to read. It's actually gonna be a series of five to seven posts that talk about all this. But the guy talked to him about the idea of you can't control the outcome of the game, especially against a team like Ohio State at that point.

There's not going to be a lot of things that you can control that are going to affect the actual outcome of the game. But what he asked him to focus on was every play, and every play lasts four to six seconds, and there's 50 to 70 plays in every football game. And if you can do your job and coach the play and make sure that the people, the players who are involved in that play are performing to the best of their ability, they're giving their best effort, they understand the assignment. They know exactly what the expectations are for them and they execute well. Even if you lose the play, the leadership that you have invested in these people is going to bring them forward, help them progress, help them get better as players and as humans. and maybe, just maybe, if you put together enough great plays, you can win the game.

And Michigan State ended up winning that game by four points. Again, twenty point underdogs. He shifted the way he focused his coaching to be about not the outcome of the game, the transaction that they were trying to accomplish, but the individual efforts and the team effort for every four to six seconds of live play during the course of that game.

And it really, really spoke to me, but I wanted to press on it because transformational leadership is a well-worn path. It's been researched and studied. And there were some things about it that I didn't fully align with. and I originally started researching it from the perspective of transformational leadership versus servant leadership. And what I've learned is they're very compatible, and there's one piece of the puzzle that I think makes not only Nick Saban as a leader great, but the methodology of transformational leadership that actually became what he called the process. And I'll talk in depth about it in the journal series. he brought care to the table. And you may look at this guy from the outside in and he's always angry and loud and things like that. But one thing I realized as I researched the story is his players still call him today. these are guys that have won championships 15, 20, 25 years ago and they still call this man when they need help, when they need to get clarity on a topic. And that tells me something. That tells me that it was more than just trying to push them to win a championship. He was truly investing in them, helping them become better men. And the impact of that I think has had a huge impact on all these guys' lives. Not perfect. There's guys that have had significant life failures that were under Nick's leadership. That's one outcome that he can't control. But what he could do is control how he was investing these people every day in practice in the game. And for me it came back to care.

At the end of the day, I think this guy really cared about his people. He wanted to see them get better, not just on the field and off the field. And that is something that I couldn't love anymore. I mean, it's just it's who I am, it's who I always have been. It's the stories that I have tried to tell in my writing and hope to get better at communicating to you all on video. so I really look forward to getting this series out. There's so much depth to it.

I originally thought it was a single post talking about a guy that I had a lot of respect for and a form of leadership that maybe I didn't align with. And what I've learned about transformational leadership, when you bake care into that equation, it can have a huge impact on the outcome of a human's life. And if you can affect a human's life, they're going to perform better in every aspect of their life. They're going to have greater opportunities that present them. And if we take that out of the context of investing in people just as part of your life, but as part of your organization or even in your own family, seeing them get better and progress is going to make the entity that you're leading get better. And if the entity that you're leading gets better, we know what comes from that real legitimate progress that can change the outcome of not only the business itself, but you as the leader and even have an impact on your community. So again, I'm really excited about that series and where it's headed.

and the last thing I want to share with you is I am getting ready to post the August devotional series. I don't know how many of you are following it. There's 250 to 300 that are consistently reading it from what I can see in the analytics. And it's dealing with the subject of accountability and that is something that continues to increase in value for me. I've done my best throughout my life to hold myself accountable to those that I can trust are going to be honest with me and lead me down a good path. I gotta say this, I've never made a decision in my life without that. not one. and it has been a very foundational thing for me. And as I've spent the time over the last 30 days or so researching it from a biblical perspective, I just think it's something that we all need. and again, I don't care what your beliefs are. I really don't. but the idea that you're going to put yourself in a position where people who are wiser or more experienced than you who can ask you hard questions and challenge you and ask for a different outcome from you is something that I just I believe needs to be a part of more of our lives. it's also a role that I fill for a few people. I have six or eight people that I meet with on a regular basis from a mentorship perspective. And I have so much fun in those conversations. it's great to see the impact. I still feel like I'm a bit of an imposter even though I've got a track record. but I have these conversations with people and the response that they give me in return, I just had one this morning with an amazing friend. and he listed off the changes that he's been able to make in his life through those conversations. so whether it's me or whether it's somebody else in your life, I just want to encourage you all to take some time and just know that you don't have to have it all figured out. And if you've got challenges, find people that you trust. Find people that are wiser than you. And I promise you there are always people wiser than you. If you think you've got it all figured out, that's a problem. But find people that can invest in you. Find people that can challenge you. Find people that can encourage you. The same input consistently over time generates the same output. And sometimes we have to change the way we do things to make a change in our lives.

So I think I'm gonna wrap this up. I rambled on a little bit longer than I thought. So new podcast format coming, new episodes with guests coming, some new journal series that I'm writing and I'm really excited about. And I just hope again that this is helpful for you all and maybe it guides you in some way. and if it is, if the work that I'm doing, if the writing I'm doing, if this podcast eventually gets consistent enough so it can be a help for you, I want to hear it. Please reach out. Please share your stories with me. Please be critical. Not afraid of that either. If I say something stupid, I don't mind people telling me that. but please communicate. Please reach out. I'm here and everything I'm doing right now is trying to put me in a position where I can help people around me continue to get better and I hope that's you. We'll see you guys next time.
key_takeaways: Transformational leadership and servant leadership are more compatible than they appear — the piece that connects them is care
Coach the play, not the outcome — every play lasts four to six seconds and the investment you make in people during each one is what carries them forward
I have never made a single decision in my life without accountability. Not one.
The same input consistently over time generates the same output — if you want a different output you have to change the input
There are always people wiser than you — find them

docs.title: The Archetype Original Podcast Season 1 Episode 1
docs.summary: Leadership has a wake. Not sometimes. Always. In this episode I use the water, the boat, and the wave to explain what servant leadership actually looks like before it ever has a name. One idea. One story.
show_notes: The science of water and the brain — Wallace Nichols, Blue Mind, and why cortisol drops when you are near water
The default mode network — the same state as deep meditation and creative flow, triggered by proximity to water
The wake a boat leaves at every speed, from idle to on plane, and why it never stops moving until it hits something
4,400 pounds of ballast, why it goes in before anyone surfs, and what happens without it
Teaching someone to surf from the wheel — the full coaching sequence before the boat moves and after
Motor learning consolidation — why the brain keeps building the movement pattern after the session ends
The three things servant leadership is not: permissiveness, self-destruction, and soft
Robert Greenleaf on stewardship and the real test of servant leadership
Chapter 23 of Accidental CEO, the sustainable servant, and why capacity is infrastructure not indulgence
Google Project Aristotle, psychological safety, and what the highest performing teams actually had in common
Serve each other. Serve our clients. What that phrase meant at Midwestern Interactive and why it worked
Non-revenue generating roles, why production requires support, and what happens to teams that know they are cared for
docs.body:
Leadership has a wake. Not sometimes. Always.

I started this episode on the shore. Water that calms the brain, backed by science, across cultures, across geographies. Dr. Wallace Nichols spent years documenting it. He called it the Blue Mind. Dopamine rises. Oxytocin rises. Cortisol drops. The brain shifts into the same state it reaches in deep meditation and creative flow. I felt it long before I could explain it.

Then I took you to the boat. The glassy water ahead that looks untouched and perfect. The wake behind it that is anything but. How it builds from idle to full throttle. How it rolls outward and does not stop until it hits something. The dock you passed ten minutes ago. The boat in the next channel. The people closest to the hull.

Then the wave. Four thousand four hundred pounds of ballast loaded before anyone gets in the water, because without the weight there is no wave. My wife Carie and I love to teach people to surf. We start before the boat moves. We give them everything they need to know before things get loud and chaotic. We talk them through every stage from the wheel. We work to pull them into the smooth side of the wave. And when they find it and drop the rope and the wave carries them forward on its own, the whole boat changes.

That is the picture. What you watched on that boat was not a watersports lesson.

The water is the environment a servant leader is trying to build. The wake is every leader's reality, whether they look back or not. The wave is what becomes possible when a leader decides to use what they create on purpose, for someone else.

Standards. Stewardship. Presence. Not as concepts. As something you can now see on the water.
docs.transcript:
Bart Paden (00:09)
Hey there, my name's Bart Paden and this is the Archetype Original Podcast episode one.

Let's see if we can do this. I love being on the water. I love being in it. I love being around it. It brings my heart peace when I let it. That is a big challenge for me. It always has been. I'm a thinker. Quiet has a tendency to let my brain run, and it can run really fast. Stillness has the same effect. Even pauses in my own speech allow a hundred rabbit trails to present themselves. Even when my body is tired, I roll over to go to sleep and my brain fills the silence.

Next thing you know, it's three AM and I'm still fending off the invasive thoughts. It's also a problem for an episode like this, at least the one I recorded last week. I'm not afraid to be transparent about it. I had multiple sections, I had multiple thoughts, and I had a challenging time wrangling them into a coherent show. This episode is one idea and one story. My mind may still want to go somewhere else, but I'm not going to let it.

I'm going somewhere with this and I believe it will help you if I can pull it off. So I said the phrase when I let it.

Have you ever sat on the shore of a large body of water? Maybe had your toes in the sand on the beach, hiked to a mountain glacier fed lake, and saw the deep, clear blue water. It's frigidly cold. Maybe stood on the bank of a river flowing wherever it was supposed to go. Everyone loves a waterfall, right? When I'm in those places, the water speaks to me. When I let it.

In time I can let my mind calm down, let it pause, let it take a break, and I find peace. The sounds, the reflections, the movement. I did a little digging to see if there was a reason for that, and science actually has affirmed it. A marine biologist named Wallace Nichols, doctor Wallace Nichols, spent years documenting what water does to the human brain. He called it the blue mind. And what he found is not subtle.

When you are near, in, on, or around water, your brain chemistry measurably shifts. Dopamine rises, that is the neurotransmitter tied to reward and motivation. Oxytocin rises, that is the one tied to trust and connection. Cortisol, the primary stress hormone, drops. For someone like me who carries high stress in my system all the time, that last one matters a great deal.

I have been fighting elevated cortisol for years. Water is one of the few things that actually moves the needle on it without a prescription. But here's the part that I find most interesting. Nichols found that being around water pushes the brain toward a state called the default mode network. If that sounds clinical, let me translate it. It is the same neurological state your brain reaches during deep meditation or during creative flow.

If you've ever been in a design session or a stretch of focused work where two hours passed like 20 minutes and the ideas were just arriving without effort, that is the default mode network. That is your brain in the state where it does its best thinking, its deepest processing, and the most genuine rest.

Nichols found this pattern across cultures and across geographies. It's not a Western experience or something that only happens on a beach vacation. It is human. We are wired for it. Science caught up to what most of us already knew we felt. Water does something to your soul. And I believe it was created to do exactly that. Some of you have seen the water in that early morning state when everything goes to glass?

All the boats are gone, everything calms. You can see the reflection of the trees, the skyline, the clouds sitting still on the surface like a mirror. Mornings and I are still negotiating whether we are going to get along. We never have. But that glass shows up in the evenings too, and is worth being there when it does.

On a cold morning the water looks different, darker. The splash on the shore becomes more of a thud. The density changes when it's cold and you can feel it, even hear it differently. There is something calming even in that for me, something that says slow down.

The glass, the cold, the rain on the roof of a marina, hitting the leaves of the trees, splashing on the surface, all of it speaks. I cannot always explain why. I just know that when I let it, something in me settles that does not settle anywhere else. Water speaks to humans. It was created to do so. But I want to talk about something specific that happens on the water. I want to talk about what a boat leaves behind.

Hang with me here. When you're driving a boat, you have to watch what you're doing or where you're going. That much is obvious. What is less obvious is what's happening behind you. On a glassy day with no wind, no other boats, eyes ahead, everything can appear untouched and perfect. The surface in front of you looks like it has not been touched. Like you are the only thing out there and the world is waiting, still and quiet for you to move through it.

When you take a moment to look back over your shoulder, the image behind you is dramatically different. The wake behind a boat is not peaceful and perfect. It can be absolute chaos. You can move without much of a wake. It's called idle speed. We use it going into a marina, around docks, and in tight spaces where other people and other boats are close. It is slow and deliberate. The engine is barely humming. The boat sits heavy in the water. You can have a full conversation at normal volume.

Almost no impact on the water around you, but you are not going anywhere. And everyone on the boat knows it. When you get clear and open the throttle up, everything changes. The water is where you see the impact first. The spray off both sides. The hull dropping at the back as the bow comes up.

The wake behind you begins to build immediately, wide and steep, rolling out in both directions. Anyone nearby can see it and feel it before they hear anything different from the engine. The wake in those moments is at its worst. Unpredictable. It reaches across the channel and rolls into whatever is in its path. You push through that and the boat gets up on plane. When it happens, it's one of the better feelings on the water.

The bow levels out, you go from looking at the sky to looking at the horizon. The engine settles into a slower, steadier tone. The ride smooths, the wake behind you changes too. It's still there, but it's no longer the chaos of acceleration. It settles into something more consistent as the boat finds its speed. But here's the thing.

Even on plane, when everything feels smooth and controlled up front, there is still a wake. Look behind you. It is there. And it keeps moving. It rolls outward. It does not stop until it hits something. The shoreline across the water felt it. It does not disappear because you found your stride.

It does not ask your permission, it does not wait for you to acknowledge it. It just goes. Responsible boaters understand the damage a wake can do to the environment and to the things it reaches. We have to own our wake.

And now I want to tell you what we do with it on purpose. My wife and I love to surf behind our boat. Before we do, before anyone gets in the water, I put 4,400 pounds of ballast in the boat. Bags of water distributed throughout the hull specifically to shape the wave we are about to create. The weight is what makes the wave surfable. Without it, the boat just makes a wake. With it, it makes something a person can stand on.

Remember that zone just before the boat gets on plane? That is where we surf. We do it on purpose. The boat is designed to create that displacement, to dig in and throw a wave. But it only works because we know what we're doing with it. We stay far enough away from shore. We protect the people around us from what we are creating. In the wrong hands, in the wrong place, that same energy is dangerous.

My wife and I also love to teach people how to surf. Sometimes for us, teaching is much more fun than dropping into a wave ourselves.

We start before the boat ever moves. We get the rider in the water, we hand them a rope, we place their heels on the board, and then we give them everything they need to know before it happens. Hold the rope like this, both hands. Feet right here on the board, bend your knees and keep them bent. The board is not going to float away, don't worry. Arms straight. Don't pull back on the rope.

Let the boat do the work. You're not stronger than it is. When you feel the pressure on your heels, push into it. You want to feel the board pop up under your feet. Keep those knees bent. Do not extend your legs. Arms straight. Then we go back to the wheel.

And while the boat is coming up to speed, we are still talking to the rider. The boat is in gear now. You're going to feel the rope get tight. When you feel that, push down with your heels. Let the board come up. Keep your legs bent and your arms straight. When I see that board kick up, I'm going to give it more. I need you to be strong right now. Everything tight. Arms, legs, core. As you come up, you will feel the board want to rise. Keep those legs bent. Now stand up and rotate your hips.

Then everything gets loud and hard and chaotic all at once. The rope goes tight, the water rushes, the board wants to go sideways and most people fight it. They pull with their arms because it feels like control. They lean the wrong way because leaning away from the chaos feels like the right answer. They try to stand too early because standing looks like winning. Every instinct in that moment is wrong.

Not everyone gets up the first time. I did not. It took me three weeks of consistent effort before it clicked. But what Carie and I watch over and over again is that the human brain keeps working on it after they get out of the water.

The second and third time someone tries, even weeks apart, something is different. The body has been processing it. There is science behind this. It's called motor learning consolidation. The brain does not stop building the movement pattern just because the session ended.

During sleep especially, the brain replays and encodes physical sequences it has been working on, which means the person who struggled badly on Saturday is often noticeably better two weeks later without a single practice session in between. We have seen it enough times that we expect it now. I actually had some people on our boat not too long ago and that was the conversation. We took them out in the morning and some of them struggled and by afternoon their brain had processed enough that they were able to actually get up successfully. It was really cool to see that in real life.

When someone finally gets up, it's not immediately peaceful. The wave is still building. Every muscle is working. The water is spraying. The boat is loud. The wave underneath them is alive and moving and making decisions they cannot fully predict. We are calling to them from the boat, relax, shake it out, just stand there. Don't do anything else yet. After a few seconds, you can see it change. The shoulders come down, the grip loosens, the face changes. The fight shifts.

They are still in the middle of everything. The frothy white water on one side of the wave, the roar of the motor, sometimes the music going, and I like to play it loud. Chaos in every direction, but right where they are standing, something different is happening. There are two sides to a wave. One is foamy and chaotic, the other smooths out. We work from the boat to pull the rider into the smooth spot, moving that boat a few degrees, calling out to them to hold position. When they land in it, the whole experience changes. They can feel the difference between where they were and where they are. Peace inside the chaos. Progress without the fight.

Then we work on putting them in control of the board. Your front foot is the gas, your back foot is the brake, your toes and heels steer. Subtle movements, not big ones. Balance is where the peace is. Find it and hold it.

Once they have that, we work on getting the rope slack. When the wave is carrying them and the rope is no longer pulling them forward, we tell them to drop it. Let the wave push you. And when they do, the whole boat changes. You can feel it in everyone. Something gets said, something gets shouted, and that is enough. This is the picture and the proof of what is possible.

Now I've got to connect everything I just said to leadership because that's what this podcast is all about.

What you just watched in your head on that boat was not a water sports lesson. It was a picture. The water we started in is the environment a servant leader is trying to build. The place where things calm down, where the noise settles, where people can actually think and find their footing. That's not an accident. That is something the leader creates on purpose. The same way the water creates it for us when we let it.

The wake is every leader's reality. You are always creating something behind you. Always. The view from the front of the boat can look like smooth water for miles. Clear, open, nothing in the way. But what is behind you is the truth. Leaders who only look forward, who only chase the next deal, the next number, the next client, they never look back. The wake is massive and nobody is watching it. And the people closest to that boat feel every bit of it, whether the person driving it ever knows or not.

The wave is what changes when the leader decides to look. When they stop treating what they create as something that just happens and start treating it as something they are responsible for, they load the ballast, they position the boat, they use what they are producing on purpose for someone else. The chaos does not go away, but the leader is managing it now instead of ignoring it.

The rider in the water is the person on your team, and everything we did from the moment we handed them the rope was leadership. The coaching before the boat moved was standards. Clear expectations before anyone asked for them. The communication from the wheel as things got loud was presence. Watching in every direction while staying connected to the person in the wave. Moving the boat to put them in the right position was stewardship. Using what you built to serve the person inside of it.

That is servant leadership, not as a concept, as something you have now seen and felt. The name just came last.

I want to talk to you about what it is not, because people get three things wrong about it every time. Servant leadership is not permissiveness. No standards. Anything goes. People do whatever they want. That is not servant leadership. Look at what we did on the boat. We gave the rider the full set of instructions before the boat ever moved. Hold the rope like this, feet here, arms straight, push with your heels, keep those knees bent. That was not optional, that was the standard. And we held it because we knew what the rider needed to be able to do when things got loud and fast. You cannot serve someone through chaos if you have not set clear expectations for what they are supposed to do in it.

I grew up in a design world and I cut my teeth early working for organizations with extremely high standards. I'm not going to name drop, but you would know them. I was being asked to move elements on the screen two pixels, two tiny dots on a monitor with millions of them. They did not relent. They knew exactly how they wanted things built, and they held to it. I grew to love that standard. I brought that into the way that I lead.

A standard is not a punishment. It is clarity and clarity is a form of care. You do not get the culture you preach. You get the culture your environment produces. You can stand in a room and tell people who you are and what you believe. What matters is whether your actions confirm it. Culture is built on what you repeat, not what you announce.

Robert Greenleaf, the man who gave servant leadership its name and its framework, wrote about stewardship as the core responsibility of a leader, not the task, not the revenue, the people. He said the best test of servant leadership is whether the people being served grow as persons, whether they become healthier, wiser, freer, more autonomous while they are under your care. That test requires a standard. It requires the leader to know what growth looks like and to hold the environment to it. Permissiveness is not care. It is avoidance dressed up as kindness. Real care has a standard behind it.

Servant leadership is not self-destruction. Before we surf, we load 4,400 pounds of ballast into that boat. Without that weight, there is no wave. But here is what does not work. You cannot keep loading the boat indefinitely and expect it to perform. There is a point where the weight becomes the problem, where the boat stops being a surf boat and becomes something that is just trying to stay above the waterline. Leadership works the same way.

A leader who takes on unlimited burden for the people around them is not serving. They are sinking. And a boat that cannot stay afloat cannot create a wave for anyone.

I failed at this. I took on so much for the people around me that I was operating from empty. My body showed it, my labs showed it, I could not breathe right in certain moments. I woke up in the middle of the night with panic attacks and did not understand where they were coming from. I was trying to do a good thing, and I went past the point where it was sustainable. Chapter twenty three of my book Accidental CEO is called the sustainable servant. The whole premise is this: servant leadership is not martyrdom, it is stewardship.

That includes stewardship of yourself, your capacity, your sleep, your health, your spiritual life, your margin. Those are not luxuries. They are the infrastructure that allows you to show up for the people you lead. If you burn the engine out trying to rescue everyone else, the mission loses you. And that is not noble, that is negligent.

Modern research backs this up consistently. Burnout is not a character flaw. It is a design flaw. It happens when the system around the leader rewards endless output and never protects recovery. Neuroscience has shown that sleep deprivation impairs judgment at the same level as alcohol impairment. You would not lead a room at .08. Do not lead it on four hours of sleep either. Capacity is not indulgence, it is infrastructure. Guard it like the asset that it is.

Servant leadership is not soft. Think about what I was doing from that boat. Watching in every direction at once. Reading the water, the wave, and the rider simultaneously, coaching constantly, making small adjustments nobody else can see. Knowing when to push and when to wait, being willing to move the boat to create conditions someone else needs even when we cannot explain exactly what we are doing in the moment. That is not soft. That is some of the most focused and demanding work that I do.

Servant leadership is probably the most demanding form of leadership I know of. The leaders who do it well are not soft. They are caring more than the people around them ever know. Holding a standard when it is uncomfortable is hard. Protecting someone when it costs you something is hard. Staying present when everything in you wants to look away is hard. Empowering someone to the point where they can drop the rope and the wave carries them, that takes patience and skill and sustained attention that most leadership models never ask for.

Google spent two years studying 180 teams trying to understand what made the highest performing ones different. They expected the answer to be skill, experience, or talent distribution. It was not. The single strongest predictor of team performance was psychological safety. The feeling inside the team that they could speak up, take a risk, make a mistake, and not be punished for it. Psychological safety is not an accident. It is built by a leader who is paying attention. A leader who is present, a leader who creates the conditions for it the same way we create conditions on that wave.

I will be making the case for servant leadership for the rest of my career. It is not weakness, it is the hardest work there is. So what is it? Three words. Standards, stewardship, and presence. I was living all three before I had words for them. The definition did not create the practice. The practice revealed the definition.

Standards are non-negotiable lines. The instruction before the boat moves, how we treat people, how we deliver work, how we protect the culture around us. We had a manual at Midwestern Interactive. We called it the Midwestern Way at one point. Real lines that people could go find, real people they could go talk to, real expectations lived out every single day. You do not get the culture you preach, you get the culture your environment produces. Culture is built on what you repeat, not what you announce, and it is revealed most clearly when it is under pressure. That is when you find out if what is on the wall is actually in the room.

Stewardship means holding something in trust that belongs to more than you. When you are leading a group of people, you are literally holding their lives in your hands. That is heavy. Your responsibility is not the task. It is not even the profitability of the business. It is the people. I held this with open hands, not clenched fists. When people wanted to leave, even great people I did not want to lose, I wanted them to find success wherever they were going. Keeping someone who does not want to be there is not stewardship. Caring about their growth as a human even after they are gone is. Research from Gallup has shown consistently that employees who feel genuinely cared for by their leaders are more than three times more likely to be engaged. Not managed. Cared for. That is the difference entirely. If you support your team, the rest comes. They will be hungry. They will move fast. They will build the thing you are trying to build together. You will not be doing it alone.

Presence means showing up in the room, not as a celebrity, as a steady hand. The leader who walks in like a high-flying fighter pilot, fast and loud and always moving. I am not impressed by that. I never have been. I want to see someone with a steady hand, someone who is actually there, not listening to respond, listening to understand. An open door policy means nothing if you are not actually present when someone walks through the door. If someone brings you a hard thing and you are listening to defend yourself, you have already lost them. The ideology is the same in every room. The boardroom, the dinner table, the marriage. The people are different. The stakes vary. The dynamic is identical. Leadership is not defined by what is produced. It is defined by what is experienced by the people inside it.

If you grow people, you grow the organization. If you use people, you lose it. I believe it. It is not a slogan. I feel it like gravity.

We had another phrase inside Midwestern Interactive. It was internal to us, something we lived by every day in how we made decisions. It was serve each other, serve our clients. It was in the culture manual. Most importantly it was in the behavior of us and our people. We had worked hard to build a culture around it from the beginning. A belief that if we took care of each other first, we would have the capacity to take care of our clients in a way nobody running on empty ever could. And that turned out to be true.

There is a belief in some business circles that non-revenue generating roles are a cost problem. That the people not directly producing billable work are a drag on the organization. I have never believed that. I could not believe it and also believe what I just told you about servant leadership. You cannot surf behind a boat with no ballast. The wave does not exist without the weight that shapes it. Production requires support always. The engineer who is not also drowning in administrative work produces better code. The designer who has a project manager clearing the path ships better work. The team that is fed in the middle of the workday, not as a perk, but as a statement that they matter enough to take care of their body while they are here, that team carries a pace that would break any team built around the assumption that people are just their output.

We built infrastructure inside the company specifically to reduce friction for the people doing the work. Project managers whose job was to clear the path for engineers and designers. Administrative staff whose job was to make sure the technical people were not also drowning in things that had nothing to do with the technical work. Those roles were not revenue generating in the direct sense, but I did not care. Supporting the people doing the work is the work. In some companies, people in those roles are even told that there are limits to how far they can advance within the organization because of it. That is not servant leadership. It is also not how real successful businesses are built.

We fed our people. We invested in their growth. If a certification would help someone go further, we paid for it. We created space in the week, not just for production, but for people. The 80-20 principle was real for us. If a hundred percent of effort goes into production, you leave no room for progress. People burn out, growth stalls, creativity disappears. When we pulled back from chasing productivity at all costs, productivity actually went up, not down, up. That pattern has been replicated in research repeatedly. When people feel seen, supported, and given margin to be human, they work harder, they stay longer, and they bring more of themselves to their work.

I often remember walking into our office and seeing people gathered around a screen working on a problem. Not because anyone asked them to, not because the process required it, but because we had built a culture where people wanted to solve problems together and had the safety to do it. We pushed hard internally against people being isolated on islands. Context was shared. Problems were surfaced. Nobody was left alone with something they could not handle. That is not something you mandate. That is something you grow. And when you grow it, the whole environment shifts.

Our culture unified everyone in a way I have rarely seen since. I do not know if you have ever lived inside an environment that was truly on the same page, but I can tell you it was something beautiful. Those were the happiest days of my business life. And the client growth that followed was real and it was rare. I am humble enough to understand that place and that time was not common. It was built. And it was built because we decided early that people matter more than numbers. And if we served each other first, the numbers would follow. And they did.

The team could carry a pace that would break any team built any other way, because they knew they would be cared for, because the leader was watching in every direction. Because when the wave got chaotic, someone was at the wheel working to put them in the smooth spot. And eventually they dropped the rope. The wave carried them. That is what it looks like when it works.

I started this episode on the shore. Water that brings peace when you let it in. A brain that finally gets quiet when the conditions are right, a world that science now confirms was wired for exactly this kind of rest. I took you to a boat because I believe leadership has a wake. Not sometimes, always. And the leaders who do the most damage are often the ones who never look back. They are moving fast, eyes forward, water smooth ahead of them, and behind them the wake is rolling into everything and everyone within reach.

But I also took you to the wave because I believe it is possible to do something intentional with what you create, to load the ballast, to position the boat, to stand at the wheel with your eyes in every direction and coach someone through the chaos you built until they find the smooth side of it, until they can stand on it, until they can let go of the rope and let the wave carry them forward.

That is servant leadership. It is not soft, it is not permissive, and it is not self-destruction. The hardest form of leadership I know, lived out by people who are willing to look back, own what they leave behind, and use it for someone else.

Standards, stewardship, presence. Not as concepts. As something you have now seen on the water and can recognize the next time you walk into a room with people in it who are counting on someone to be at the wheel.

The view from the front of the boat can look like smooth water for miles. It is what is behind you that tells the real story. Take a look back at your wake. Own what you see, then decide what kind of wave you want to build.

And that's the episode. I hope you all enjoyed it. I hope you all gained something from it. We'll see you next time.
key_takeaways: The view from the front of the boat can look like smooth water for miles — it is what is behind you that tells the real story
Servant leadership is not permissiveness, not self-destruction, and not soft — it is the most demanding form of leadership there is
Standards, stewardship, and presence are not concepts. They are something you can now see on the water.
You cannot surf behind a boat with no ballast. A leader running on empty cannot build a wave for anyone.
When the wave carries them and they drop the rope, that is what it looks like when it works

docs.title: The Archetype Original Podcast Season 1 Episode 0
docs.summary: Hey, I'm Bart Paden. This is my first podcast. Ever. Thirty-three years in business, a software company sold in 2022, and a realization that the decisions I made to put people first weren't original — just rare. This is the beginning of that conversation out loud.
show_notes: 33 years building companies, from a home office to 104 people, sold in 2022
Why servant leadership is a hard stance, not a soft one
The four books behind the Archetype Original corpus
What The Room taught me about honesty inside leadership teams
The Archetype Leadership Index and what it's built to measure
What's coming next: solo episodes and guest conversations
docs.body:
Hey, I'm Bart Paden. This is my first podcast. Ever.

Thirty-three years in business, starting in Carthage and Joplin, Missouri, building a software company from the ground up after I got hooked on the internet back in 1993. I sold that company in 2022, and that sale put me through something close to an identity crisis. Who was I if not the guy building that thing?

What I found when I went looking wasn't new. The decisions I'd made to put people first weren't original. Just rare. I talk through what servant leadership actually means to me, why it's a hard stance and not a soft one, and why the success of that company belonged to the 104 people who showed up for it, not to me.

I walk through the four books behind everything I've built. Accidental CEO, my story and the methodology that came out of it. Remaining Human, an argument for leading like a person in an age of AI. The Room, built on something that shook me — no leader ever has a fully honest room. And The Leadership Gap, still unpublished, tied to the Archetype Leadership Index I'm building to measure the distance between how leaders see themselves and how their teams actually experience them.

I close on the thing I believe most. If you grow people, you grow the organization. If you use people, you lose it. Two kinds of episodes are coming, solo and guest, and I want you in this with me. Ask questions. Push back.
docs.transcript:
Bart Paden (00:11)
Hey, my name is Bart Paden and this is the intro episode to the Archetype Original podcast. Here we are. Yeah, so I'm brand new to this. This is really the first time I've ever sat down to do something in this arena. And I'm really uncomfortable. So I hope you'll bear with me as I figure it out and learn my way through this. My hope is that I can communicate clearly enough that you will learn and grow, just like I have throughout my entire career.

Got ideas, I've got things I want to share. We'll just see how well I do when it comes to communicating them. Yeah. So let me give you a little intro about me and who I am and what I've done with my career to this point and then we'll talk about what this thing's gonna be and where we're headed with it and also a little bit about what I've been doing over the last three or four years.

Been in business for thirty-three years, in around the Carthage, Missouri and Joplin, Missouri areas. I'm an entrepreneur, I'm a builder. Early on I knew that this was the case, even coming out of college. I knew that was the direction that I wanted to head.

I was introduced to the internet in nineteen ninety-three, nineteen ninety-four by a couple of professors at Missouri Southern State University in Joplin. Really inspired me to take a look at what that technology might become and it really spoke to me and I jumped on it and used what I was learning about the internet to help put me through college and provide for my family even at a young age.

So this journey, yeah, it's been thirty-three give or take years. And it's been enjoyable. It's had lots of challenges, lots of ups, really big ups and some pretty significant downs. I learned a lot about what I care about.

What was most interesting to me is that the internet inspired me to get involved in it, but what I learned from building companies in that space, I cared about the people way more. And I love the idea of developing humans and helping them grow and get better and find success, whether it be at work or at home in their personal lives.

I developed an unknown passion for leadership. And I say that because I'm probably the least well-read leader out there. I chose to forge my own path. I wanted to do it the way that I saw fit me and what I was trying to build. I didn't want to be someone who regurgitated a bunch of stuff that other people had done.

Not because what they did was wrong, just I wanted to do it my way. And maybe that was short sighted, maybe I made some mistakes that I shouldn't have made, but I really think looking back I made the right decision.

In twenty twenty-two I had probably the largest shift in my business life. I had built a software company from the ground up beginning in nineteen ninety-three. In twenty-two I sold that company to my partner and stepped away from the industry a little bit and took a break. That sale put me in a situation that I didn't realize I was gonna be in. A little bit of what I'll call an existential crisis, but it really wasn't as deep as that. But I did have a lot of questions about who I was and where my identity was. What I had built — was it something that was worth remembering, the work that I had done. Did it leave a legacy behind that mattered?

So like I always have done, I figured it out. I started doing research. I started asking a lot of questions and I started learning again that the decisions that I made to take care of people, they were not brand new paths. They were relatively well-worn paths in a lot of situations. They're just rare in business.

I believe wholeheartedly that servant leadership is not a soft phrase. It's a very challenging way to lead, it's a very difficult stance to take. I believe putting your people as more valuable than the task that you're asking them to take on can really change how a business functions. I believe that it can create sustainable long-term growth that is extremely stable in spite of things like pandemics and economic downturns and all sorts of unforeseen issues that have come up over the course of my thirty-three years doing this. And I think it all points back to how you take care of your people.

We had a relatively robust staff, very intelligent, very committed to their task, and we were asking a lot from them. But I think we provided the right level of support and care for them in those moments that allowed them to stay engaged, stay hungry, get rest when they needed it, and continue to move forward. And I had a team of 104 people around me at the peak of my time in that business where I was confident we could run through just about any brick wall together. And I say that intentionally. I was one who never led from the back. I was one that led shoulder to shoulder with my people. They knew they could count on me. They knew I had ears that were open to hear, not just to respond, but to actually understand.

And I value those conversations. I still look forward to the moments when I get to have those conversations with some of my people today. Some of my former people — they're still my people. That's something you learn about me. I care a lot. And if you're connected to me in any form, it's not easy for me to let go.

So yeah. I care about people. I believe in servant leadership. I've built the company that I've founded on that idea of servant leadership. I believe it is the best leadership methodology. I was connected to about thirteen different industries as I worked my way through the previous part of my career. So I've had a lot of experience. I've sat at tables and rooms with people who run businesses that were not like mine, who were in completely different industries, and I learned a lot from working with them.

One of the things that you figure out when you're building software is you realize you have to learn the business logic for any company that you're working with. You have to understand how they communicate, how they manage their information and how they run their business because most of the time we were building systems that supported that. And I think that was really beneficial from an education standpoint. I can sit here today and speak competently about the businesses that I've been connected to and I believe that it positions me to help people going forward.

Archetype Original is, loosely, a consulting business, loosely a mentorship company, loosely a leadership company. Since I began down this path, I've written over 350,000 words. And I'm very, very proud of that effort. And it's continuing to grow. My goal by the end of this calendar year is to have over half a million words in the corpus that is the brain behind the AI that I've built for my business.

That corpus includes four books. The first book being Accidental CEO. It is my story. It's fifty percent my journey, the other fifty percent is the methodology that I espoused, the fundamentals of servant leadership that I could identify during a specific part of the timeline in my life that I really felt helped me lead, helped people grow and develop. And I think it was the foundation for why the company had so much success. And I want to be real clear — that company didn't have success because of my effort. That company had success because we had a team of people that were committed to working together and helping each other and growing each other and supporting the mission and vision that was presented to them. And that comes from culture. That comes from leadership. That comes from a posture of understanding that you're there to take care of those around you as a leader.

I believe that. And I've tried to live it out as best I can throughout my career and I think I did an okay job. You can find Accidental CEO on any bookstore out there online. It's also available on my website. I think it's a decent read. It's kind of weird to see thirty-plus years of your life condensed down into a hundred and seventy-eight pages.

I've written three other books. One of them is called Remaining Human. It's published and out there as an ebook. You can find it on my website and buy it. It basically explains that we're living in an age of AI and we have to continue to lead as humans. There are too many folks that are handing off their leadership and their leadership decisions to the machine. And I firmly believe that the machine doesn't have all the information. You have to consider a lot of the intangible stuff — and that comes through relationship, through clear communication, through transparency, through caring about your people more than the task that they're assigned to complete.

The next book I wrote is called The Room. The room is based on a realization that I had as I was doing my research. I always thought I had rooms that were fully supportive and had teams that were fully on the same page with what we were communicating as a company. And what I realized is I never had a fully honest room. I just didn't. And why? Not because my people were malicious or they didn't want to be there. It's actually because they had strings attached. And everybody does. You want to keep your job. You want to not step on the toes of the people that are leading you. You don't want to offend the founder. You want to make sure that your paycheck continues to grow.

And conversations that we would have in those rooms — I just realized that it's not fully honest. There are ways that you can lead your way through that. There are ways that you can improve communication, be more clear, be more transparent, be more present. And that's something that I think leaders are missing wholesale right now.

The last book that I've written, not published yet but coming, is called The Leadership Gap. It goes along with a platform that I built called the Archetype Leadership Index. It basically explains there's a gap between what leaders believe that they're doing as leaders and what their team members actually experience. And that gap between those two is exactly where I work.

The ALI takes survey data that we send out four times a year to your leadership and to your team members. It does a bunch of calculations and projections and forecasting, and it's fully connected to the corpus that I've built. So the intelligence behind it is truly methodology that I trust because I built it from lived experience.

There are gonna be two types of episodes. Solo episodes like this one — just me talking, sharing things that I believe should be shared. Maybe ranting, maybe rambling. And then guest episodes with people I've been talking to. Some of them you know, some of them you don't know. It's not gonna just be leadership. It won't just be business. I want to talk about life. I want to talk about what these people have accomplished, where they're headed, even the failures.

In the end the humans matter and they matter more to me than anything else I could do.

If you grow people, you grow an organization. Period. I believe that is a rule. It's a law. Just like gravity. If you use people, you're gonna lose your organization. If you believe that your people are arrows in your quiver that are designed to be spent and forgotten about, you're gonna struggle.

Leadership is about picking up the burden and carrying it for those around you. That's really what it boils down to.

I hope you engage. If you have questions, please ask them. If you want to hear something or you want to challenge something, I want you to ask it. That's what this is here for. I'm not here to say things and hide. I want to be challenged just as much as I hope to challenge and inspire you.

So there it is. The intro episode, Episode 0 of the Archetype Original Podcast. I did it.

We'll see you guys soon.
key_takeaways: Servant leadership is a demanding stance, not a soft one
Success belongs to the team, not the leader — 104 people built that company, not one person
Leadership is the burden you choose to pick up, not a title you're given

docs.title: The Room
docs.summary: Full manuscript: the structural limitation of honest rooms when consequence is present — and what exists outside them.
takeaways: No fully honest room exists when authority and consequence shape what can be said.
Healthy cultures can still filter what reaches the leader; the gap is structural.
The response is outside the organizational room — relationship without stake inside the system.
applications: Archy and site knowledge for The Room book and advisory conversations.
docs.body:
# The Room

**Bart Paden**

*Copyright 2026 by Bart Paden*

*All rights reserved. No part of this publication may be copied, reproduced, republished, translated, stored, or transmitted in any form or by any means without the prior written permission of the publisher.*

*The perspectives shared in this book are based on the author's personal experience in leadership, business, and organizational development. They are intended to challenge, inform, and inspire, not to serve as legal, financial, or professional advice.*

*Published by Archetype Original, LLC*
*Carthage, Missouri, USA*
*archetypeoriginal.com*

*First Edition*

---

## Table of Contents

- Prologue
- Chapter 1: The Room You Think You Have
- Chapter 2: They Live Inside the System
- Chapter 3: The Cost You Cannot See
- Chapter 4: What Leaders Do Instead
- Chapter 5: A Different Kind of Room
- Chapter 6: What the Room Actually Looks Like
- Epilogue
- Bibliography

---

## Prologue

I have sat in these rooms.

I have seen the looks on my team's faces. I know how uncomfortable it feels when something important goes unsaid. I also know that discomfort is not universal. Some of you reading this do not even realize your room is not fully honest. The signals are there. You have just learned to read them as something else.

This realization did not come to me early. It came while I was digging deep into the question of where leadership tends to fail without real explanation. Not the dramatic failures. The quiet ones. The decisions that felt right in the room and cost something downstream. The looks that passed between people after a meeting ended. The whispered conversations. The lone teammate who finally decided to take the risk and ask the question out loud that everyone else had been carrying silently.

What are we doing?

I am not going to tell you I figured this out years ago. I did not. This became clear to me recently, and the data supports it in ways I could not have anticipated when I started looking.

Here is what I found.

It is impossible to have a fully honest room. Not because your people are dishonest. Not because your culture is broken. Not because you have failed as a leader. But because the people in that room live inside the system your decisions shape, and no one inside a system is ever fully free of its consequences. They need their jobs. They need to provide for their families. They want to show up and believe they are moving the needle. They want to collaborate without carrying the weight of everything pressing on their lives both inside and outside the organization.

You do not want them removed from that reality. They need to be inside the system for the whole thing to work. But you need something they cannot give you from inside it.

You need a place where consequence does not follow the conversation. Where you can think out loud with someone operating at the same level you are. Where you can work through volatile situations, name what is actually happening, and say it all without concern for the impact on the people you need most.

I started asking how to fix the incomplete room. The honest answer is that you cannot fix it. That is not a failure of leadership or culture or trust. It is a structural reality. The fix is not inside the room.

It is outside of it.

Thirty-three years of building companies, leading people, making decisions under pressure, carrying the cost of the ones that did not land, and finding my way back when the ground gave way did not produce a framework or a methodology. It produced the pattern recognition that only comes from having been inside enough rooms to understand what they cannot produce on their own.

That is what prepared me for the outside room.

That is what this book is about.

That is why I wrote it.

And that is where The Room begins.

## Chapter 1
### The Room You Think You Have

You have seen it.

The glance that moves across a table before someone speaks. The Slack message that appears ten minutes after a meeting ends, the one that says something the sender did not say out loud. The hallway conversation that carries a different tone than the one that just happened in the room, more direct, more honest, more alive with the thing that actually needed to be said.

You noticed. You always notice. You did not get to where you are by being socially blind. Reading people, reading rooms, reading the space between what is said and what is meant, that is part of how you function. You have built something real. You have led people through hard seasons and good ones. You have made decisions under pressure and stood behind them. You are not naive about human behavior.

But there is a difference between sensing a room and understanding what is actually happening inside it. And that difference is costing you more than you know.

When you bring your team together to work through an idea you are still forming, you believe you are being transparent. You believe you are creating space for real input. You expect honest pushback, the kind that sharpens thinking and surfaces what you cannot see from where you sit. What you usually receive feels constructive, some affirmation, a few refinements, perhaps a light objection from someone close enough to you to risk it. You leave the meeting feeling clearer than when you walked in.

That feeling is not nothing. It reflects a real culture, real trust, real relationships built over time. In many cases the people around you are thoughtful and capable and genuinely trying to help you think well. And yet something else is happening in that room that the feeling of alignment does not capture.

It does not require a broken culture. It does not require fear-based leadership or fragile egos or people who are managing you instead of serving you. It requires only one condition that exists in every room where authority is present.

Everyone in that room lives inside the system your decisions shape.

They are not observers evaluating ideas from a neutral position. They execute your decisions. They absorb their impact downstream. They manage the morale shifts when something lands harder than expected. They field questions from their own teams. They carry the weight of what you set in motion long after the meeting ends. That reality does not make them dishonest. It makes them human. And it means the input you receive, no matter how thoughtfully offered, has already been shaped by something you cannot see from the front of the room.

The room can feel completely healthy and still be fundamentally incomplete. That gap does not announce itself. It does not show up in your culture scores or your retention numbers or the quality of the people you have built around you. It exists because of the position you hold and the consequences that flow from it, and it exists whether you are a strong leader or a weak one, whether your culture is thriving or struggling, whether your people love working for you or are simply tolerating it. The gap is structural. It is not a verdict on your leadership. But it is a reality your leadership has to reckon with.

Most leaders never consider that possibility because the signals that would reveal it are quiet and familiar and easy to mistake for something else. The light objection feels like engagement. The affirmation feels like alignment. The refinement feels like collaboration. None of those things are false. They are simply partial. They represent what the people around you were willing to put on the table given everything they were simultaneously navigating, their relationships, their responsibilities, their read of the moment, and the reality that whatever gets decided, they will still be the ones who have to live inside it.

## Chapter 2
### They Live Inside the System

I did not arrive at this understanding through failure.

That matters, because most books about leadership blind spots are written from the wreckage. A toxic culture collapsed. A team fractured. A company lost its way and someone finally figured out why. That is not this story.

The company I built grew consistently year over year, well beyond what most organizations sustain. The people around me were high-functioning, highly skilled, deeply committed, and loyal in the way that only comes from a culture built on something real. We were fortunate. Not just in the numbers, but in the team that carried them. That kind of growth creates enormous pressure, and the fact that our culture absorbed it without breaking said something about the people we had built around us. I trusted them. I respected them. I believed in what we had built together. When I walked into those rooms, I never felt at a disadvantage.

That is exactly what made this realization so disorienting.

As I studied the research on leadership and honest feedback, what actually surfaces inside organizations versus what leaders believe surfaces, I kept finding the same pattern. The leaders who struggled most with unfiltered truth were not the ones running broken cultures. They were the ones who believed, with good reason, that they had built healthy ones. Studies on what organizational psychologists call information asymmetry in hierarchical systems show that even high-trust environments systematically filter the information that reaches decision-makers. Research by James Detert and Amy Edmondson found that employees withhold information from leaders not primarily out of fear, but out of rational calculation about consequence, even in organizations they describe as psychologically safe. The calculation is not dramatic. It is quiet, constant, and largely invisible to the person at the top.

I had built psychological safety. I had built trust. I had built a culture where people knew they were seen and valued. And I was still receiving filtered input. Not because my people were dishonest. Because they were human.

---

There is a moment I return to when I try to explain this.

We had just acquired a building, fifty years old, industrial, the kind of space that looked more like a warehouse than a headquarters. Dark, grimy, carrying the residue of decades on every surface. Only someone who could see past what something was to what it could become would have chosen it. We gathered the entire company there. We walked through a year of extraordinary results, celebrated the wins, gave credit where it was due. And then we turned toward the future, toward vision, toward what we were building next.

The room went quiet in a way I was not expecting.

Not hostile. Not resistant. Just heavy.

What I intended as inspiration arrived as more pressure on people who were already pressed to their limit. Years of hard growth had cost something real. The fatigue was present in that room. I simply was not reading it correctly. I left that meeting knowing we had dropped the ball, that we had handed our people more weight when what they needed was relief.

What I understand now that I did not fully understand then is that the problem ran deeper than timing or tone. Every person in that room was living inside the system my decisions shaped. They were not evaluating the vision as independent observers who could weigh it on its merits and respond accordingly. They were absorbing it as people who would have to execute it, explain it to their own teams, manage the disruption if it created friction, and carry the weight if it fell short. They could not be fully objective about it because they lacked the one thing objectivity requires. Distance from consequence.

---

This is what the research keeps returning to, and what experience keeps confirming.

A vice president may clearly see that a decision carries risks that have not been fully thought through, risks that will show up downstream in ways that are not yet visible in the room, and still choose to raise the concern gently rather than press it hard. Not because they lack the courage to speak, but because they are already calculating what execution will look like if the decision moves forward anyway, and they know that burning relational capital on a battle they are unlikely to win is not in their interest or their team's. A director may sense that a strategic hire feels misaligned with where the organization actually is, and still hesitate to make that case forcefully because the hire carries visible sponsorship from leadership and the cost of being publicly wrong feels higher than the cost of staying quiet. A senior leader may have a better path in mind and still decide the meeting is already too far resolved to reopen, and that spending that energy on execution is more valuable than spending it on a fight over direction.

These are not weak people making weak choices. They are responsible people making calculated ones. Detert and Edmondson's research identified what they call implicit voice theories, the consistent pattern of capable, committed employees choosing not to surface concerns upward, not out of fear, but out of sophisticated and largely unconscious calculation about what their voice will actually change. That calculation accounts for relationship history, emotional tone, organizational momentum, execution burden, and a dozen other signals no culture initiative can fully override.

The person sitting across from you is simultaneously reading the emotional temperature of the room and what it signals about your receptivity, weighing whether this is a moment where pushback will genuinely shift direction or simply be heard and set aside, calculating the relational cost of pressing an issue that carries your visible investment, and considering what they will still be responsible for delivering once the meeting ends and the decision is made. None of that is manipulation. None of it requires a broken culture or a leader who punishes dissent. It requires only that they live inside the system your decisions shape, and no one inside a system is ever fully free of its consequences.

---

The realization that landed hardest was this. The healthier the culture, the harder this is to see.

In a broken culture, the filtering is visible. People go quiet when leadership enters. Conversations shift. The signals are readable to anyone paying attention. But in a healthy culture, people engage. They push back on smaller things. They ask good questions. They offer refinements. The conversation feels alive and productive. The leader leaves feeling heard. And still, the largest concerns, the sharpest risks, the alternative someone was considering but decided not to raise, those do not reliably make it to the table. Not because the culture failed. Because the system is working exactly as systems work when human beings operate inside them.

What you receive in that room is not dishonesty. It is a version of the truth that has already been shaped by consequence. The question is not whether your people trust you. Most of them do. The question is whether trust alone is enough to overcome the structural reality that everyone in that room lives inside the system your decisions shape.

For most leaders, in most rooms, it is not.

That is not a failure of leadership. It is a limitation of structure. And understanding that distinction is where everything that follows begins.
